title: Acne
text:
# Acne

**Symptoms** Acne typically appears as a mixture of comedones (blackheads and whiteheads), inflamed papules and pustules, and in more severe cases nodules or cysts. Lesions most often occur on the face, chest, and back where sebaceous glands are abundant. Affected skin may be oily and tender; severe inflammatory acne can be painful and may lead to permanent scarring and post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation. Psychological effects are common and include embarrassment, social withdrawal, anxiety, and lowered self-esteem, particularly in adolescents and young adults.

**Treatment** Treatment is staged according to severity. For mild acne, first-line therapy is topical agents: benzoyl peroxide to reduce bacteria and comedone formation; topical retinoids (tretinoin, adapalene) to normalize follicular epithelial desquamation; and topical antibiotics combined with benzoyl peroxide to reduce resistance. Moderate inflammatory acne often requires oral antibiotics (doxycycline, minocycline) for their anti-inflammatory and antibacterial effects, usually combined with topical retinoids. Hormonal therapy (combined oral contraceptives, spironolactone) is effective for women with signs of androgen excess or cyclical flares. Severe nodulocystic acne is treated with oral isotretinoin under specialist supervision because of its teratogenicity and systemic side effects; monitoring includes liver function tests and lipid profiles. Adjunctive measures include gentle skin care, avoidance of comedogenic cosmetics, sun protection, and, for scarring, dermatologic procedures such as chemical peels, microneedling, or laser resurfacing. Long-term management focuses on preventing scarring and addressing psychosocial impact.

title: Addiction (Substance Use Disorders)
text:
# Addiction (Substance Use Disorders)

**Symptoms** Addiction is characterized by compulsive use of a substance or engagement in a behavior despite harmful consequences. Core features include intense cravings, impaired control over use, tolerance (needing more to achieve the same effect), and withdrawal symptoms on cessation. Physical signs vary by substance: alcohol misuse may cause tremor, nausea, and autonomic instability; opioid dependence may present with pinpoint pupils, constipation, and sedation; stimulant misuse can cause weight loss, insomnia, and cardiovascular symptoms. Behavioral and social consequences include neglect of responsibilities, relationship breakdown, legal or financial problems, and continued use despite awareness of harm. Co-occurring psychiatric disorders (depression, anxiety, PTSD) are common and complicate treatment.

**Treatment** Effective treatment is multimodal and individualized. Initial medical stabilization (detoxification) manages acute withdrawal under supervision; benzodiazepines are used for alcohol withdrawal, and opioid withdrawal may be managed with buprenorphine or methadone. Pharmacotherapies reduce cravings and relapse risk: naltrexone and acamprosate for alcohol use disorder; buprenorphine,

methadone, and extended-release naltrexone for opioid use disorder. Psychosocial interventions are central: cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) addresses maladaptive thoughts and coping skills; motivational interviewing enhances readiness to change; contingency management uses incentives to reinforce abstinence. Residential rehabilitation programs provide structured environments for those with severe dependence. Long-term recovery often requires ongoing counseling, peer support groups (e.g., Alcoholics Anonymous), relapse prevention planning, and treatment of co-occurring mental health conditions. Family involvement and social support improve outcomes.

title: Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD)
text:
# Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD)

**Symptoms** ADHD presents with a persistent pattern of inattention and/or hyperactivity-impulsivity that interferes with functioning. Inattention symptoms include difficulty sustaining attention, careless mistakes, poor organization, forgetfulness, and avoidance of tasks requiring sustained mental effort. Hyperactivity-impulsivity includes fidgeting, inability to remain seated, excessive talking, interrupting others, and acting without considering consequences. Symptoms begin in childhood but may persist into adulthood, where inattentive symptoms and executive dysfunction (time management, planning) often predominate. ADHD frequently coexists with learning disorders, anxiety, and mood disorders.

**Treatment** Treatment combines pharmacologic and nonpharmacologic strategies. First-line medications are stimulant agents (methylphenidate, amphetamine salts) that increase catecholamine activity and improve attention and impulse control; they are effective in the majority of patients but require monitoring for appetite suppression, sleep disturbance, and cardiovascular effects. Nonstimulant options (atomoxetine, guanfacine, clonidine) are alternatives when stimulants are ineffective or contraindicated. Behavioral therapies include parent training, classroom interventions, organizational skills training, and CBT for adolescents and adults. Educational accommodations (IEP/504 plans) support academic performance. A comprehensive approach addresses comorbid conditions, sleep hygiene, and lifestyle factors such as regular exercise and structured routines.

title: AIDS (Acquired Immunodeficiency Syndrome)
text:
# AIDS (Acquired Immunodeficiency Syndrome)

**Symptoms** AIDS is the advanced stage of infection with human immunodeficiency virus (HIV), marked by severe immunosuppression and susceptibility to opportunistic infections and certain malignancies. Early HIV infection may be asymptomatic or present with a mononucleosis-like illness. As immune function declines, patients develop recurrent infections (pneumocystis pneumonia, candidiasis), chronic diarrhea, weight loss, persistent fevers, night sweats, generalized lymphadenopathy, and neurologic complications. AIDS-defining illnesses include certain opportunistic

infections and cancers such as Kaposi sarcoma and non-Hodgkin lymphoma. Laboratory markers include progressive CD4+ T-cell decline and high viral load.

**Treatment** Antiretroviral therapy (ART) is the cornerstone of HIV care and transforms HIV into a manageable chronic disease when started early and taken consistently. Modern ART regimens combine drugs from different classes (e.g., integrase inhibitors, nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitors) to suppress viral replication, restore immune function, and reduce transmission risk. Treatment is individualized based on resistance testing, comorbidities, and drug interactions. Management also includes prophylaxis and treatment of opportunistic infections, vaccination where appropriate, screening for and treating co-infections (hepatitis B/C, tuberculosis), and addressing psychosocial needs. Regular monitoring of CD4 counts and viral load guides therapy. Prevention strategies include pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP) for high-risk individuals and post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP) after potential exposure.

title: Alcoholism (Alcohol Use Disorder)
text:
# Alcoholism (Alcohol Use Disorder)

**Symptoms** Alcohol use disorder ranges from hazardous drinking to severe dependence. Symptoms include inability to limit drinking, craving, continued use despite harm, tolerance, and withdrawal symptoms (tremor, anxiety, nausea, seizures in severe cases). Chronic heavy drinking leads to medical complications: liver disease (fatty liver, hepatitis, cirrhosis), cardiomyopathy, neuropathy, pancreatitis, and increased cancer risk. Cognitive impairment and mood disorders are common. Social and occupational dysfunction, legal problems, and family disruption frequently accompany the disorder.

**Treatment** Treatment begins with assessment of severity and medical stabilization for withdrawal; benzodiazepines are commonly used to prevent severe withdrawal complications. Pharmacologic options to support abstinence include naltrexone (reduces craving and reward), acamprosate (supports abstinence), and disulfiram (produces aversive reaction to alcohol). Psychosocial interventions—CBT, motivational enhancement therapy, and mutual-help groups—are effective components of care. Integrated treatment for co-occurring psychiatric disorders improves outcomes. For advanced liver disease, referral for transplant evaluation may be necessary after sustained abstinence. Long-term follow-up, relapse prevention planning, and social support are essential.

title: Allergies (Allergic Rhinitis, Food and Drug Allergies, Atopy)
text:
# Allergies (Allergic Rhinitis, Food and Drug Allergies, Atopy)

**Symptoms** Allergic conditions manifest when the immune system reacts to otherwise harmless substances (allergens). Common symptoms include sneezing, nasal congestion, rhinorrhea, itchy and watery eyes, skin rashes (urticaria, eczema), and in severe cases angioedema or anaphylaxis. Food allergies can cause gastrointestinal symptoms, hives, and anaphylaxis. Drug allergies may present with rashes, fever, or systemic reactions. Allergic asthma presents with wheeze, cough, and breathlessness

triggered by allergens. Symptoms may be seasonal or perennial depending on the allergen.

**Treatment** Management includes allergen avoidance when feasible, pharmacotherapy, and immunotherapy. For allergic rhinitis, intranasal corticosteroids are the most effective controller therapy; oral or intranasal antihistamines relieve itching and sneezing. Leukotriene receptor antagonists can help in allergic asthma and rhinitis. For acute urticaria or mild allergic reactions, oral antihistamines and topical corticosteroids are used; anaphylaxis requires immediate intramuscular epinephrine and emergency care. Allergen immunotherapy (subcutaneous or sublingual) is effective for long-term reduction of sensitivity to inhalant allergens and can reduce medication needs. For food allergies, strict avoidance and education on emergency epinephrine use are essential. Identification of triggers through history and testing (skin prick, specific IgE) guides management.

title: Alzheimer’s Disease
text:
# Alzheimer’s Disease

**Symptoms** Alzheimer’s disease is a progressive neurodegenerative disorder characterized by gradual decline in memory, executive function, language, and visuospatial skills. Early signs include short-term memory loss and difficulty learning new information; as disease advances, patients develop disorientation, impaired judgment, behavioral changes (apathy, agitation, wandering), and loss of ability to perform activities of daily living. Neuropsychiatric symptoms such as depression, psychosis, and sleep disturbances are common. The course is progressive over years, ultimately leading to severe cognitive impairment and dependence.

**Treatment** There is no cure, but treatments can modestly slow symptom progression and improve quality of life. Cholinesterase inhibitors (donepezil, rivastigmine, galantamine) are used in mild to moderate disease to enhance cholinergic neurotransmission and may improve cognition and function. Memantine, an NMDA receptor antagonist, is used in moderate to severe stages to reduce excitotoxicity. Nonpharmacologic interventions—cognitive stimulation, structured routines, environmental modifications, and caregiver education—are critical. Management of behavioral symptoms may include behavioral strategies first; antipsychotics are reserved for severe agitation or psychosis due to risks. Addressing comorbid medical conditions, ensuring safety, and planning for long-term care needs are essential components of care.

title: Anemia
text:
# Anemia

**Symptoms** Anemia is a reduction in hemoglobin concentration or red blood cell mass, producing symptoms related to decreased oxygen delivery: fatigue, weakness, pallor, shortness of breath on exertion, palpitations, and dizziness. Severe or rapidly developing anemia can cause chest pain, syncope, or heart failure. Specific types of

anemia may have additional signs: iron-deficiency anemia can cause pica and brittle nails; hemolytic anemias may present with jaundice and dark urine; megaloblastic anemia (B12/folate deficiency) can cause neurologic symptoms such as paresthesias and gait disturbance.

**Treatment** Treatment targets the underlying cause. Iron-deficiency anemia is treated with oral iron supplementation and investigation for sources of blood loss (gastrointestinal bleeding, heavy menstruation); intravenous iron is used when oral therapy is not tolerated or absorption is impaired. Vitamin B12 deficiency requires parenteral or high-dose oral B12 replacement; folate deficiency is treated with folic acid. Hemolytic anemias may require immunosuppression for autoimmune causes, transfusions for severe anemia, or disease-specific therapies (e.g., splenectomy in select hereditary hemolytic disorders). Chronic disease–related anemia management focuses on treating the underlying illness and may include erythropoiesis-stimulating agents in selected patients with renal disease or cancer. Monitoring response with hemoglobin and reticulocyte counts guides therapy.

title: Anorexia Nervosa
text:
# Anorexia Nervosa

**Symptoms** Anorexia nervosa is an eating disorder marked by self-imposed starvation, intense fear of weight gain, and distorted body image. Patients severely restrict caloric intake, may engage in excessive exercise, purging, or laxative misuse, and often have a significantly low body weight relative to age and sex. Medical complications are widespread: bradycardia, hypotension, electrolyte disturbances, amenorrhea, osteoporosis, gastrointestinal dysmotility, and increased mortality risk from cardiac arrhythmia or suicide. Psychological features include perfectionism, denial of illness, and comorbid depression or anxiety.

**Treatment** Treatment is multidisciplinary and urgent when medical instability is present. Initial goals are medical stabilization and nutritional rehabilitation, often requiring inpatient care for severe malnutrition or electrolyte abnormalities. Refeeding must be carefully managed to avoid refeeding syndrome. Psychotherapeutic approaches include family-based therapy (especially for adolescents), cognitive behavioral therapy, and supportive psychotherapy to address distorted beliefs about weight and food. Pharmacotherapy has limited benefit for core anorexia symptoms but may treat comorbid depression or anxiety. Long-term follow-up addresses bone health, reproductive issues, and relapse prevention. Collaboration among physicians, psychiatrists, dietitians, and family members is essential.

title: Anxiety Disorders
text:
# Anxiety Disorders

**Symptoms** Anxiety disorders encompass generalized anxiety disorder (GAD), panic disorder, social anxiety disorder, specific phobias, and others. Core symptoms include excessive worry, restlessness, muscle tension, sleep disturbance, irritability, and

difficulty concentrating. Panic disorder features recurrent unexpected panic attacks—sudden surges of intense fear with palpitations, sweating, trembling, shortness of breath, and fear of losing control. Social anxiety causes marked fear of social situations and avoidance. Anxiety often coexists with depression and substance use disorders and can cause significant functional impairment.

**Treatment** Evidence-based treatment combines psychotherapy and pharmacotherapy. Cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) is first-line for many anxiety disorders and teaches cognitive restructuring, exposure techniques, and coping skills. Pharmacologic options include selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs) and serotonin-norepinephrine reuptake inhibitors (SNRIs) as first-line medications; benzodiazepines provide rapid symptom relief but are used cautiously due to dependence risk. For panic disorder, CBT with interoceptive exposure plus an SSRI is effective. Social anxiety benefits from CBT with exposure and sometimes beta-blockers for performance situations. Adjunctive strategies include relaxation training, mindfulness, sleep hygiene, and addressing comorbid conditions. Treatment is individualized and often continued for months to years to prevent relapse.

title: Back Pain
text:
# Back Pain

**Symptoms** Back pain ranges from a dull, constant ache to a sudden, sharp pain that leaves a person incapacitated. It may be localized to the lower back (lumbar), mid-back (thoracic), or upper back (cervical), and can radiate into the buttocks, legs (sciatica), or arms depending on nerve involvement. Symptoms include muscle stiffness, limited range of motion, difficulty standing or walking, and pain that worsens with certain movements or prolonged sitting. Acute back pain often follows an injury or heavy lifting; chronic back pain persists for months and may be associated with degenerative changes, spinal stenosis, or disc disease. Red flags such as fever, unexplained weight loss, progressive neurological deficits (numbness, weakness, bowel/bladder dysfunction) require urgent evaluation.

**Treatment** Initial management emphasizes conservative care: relative rest for a short period, heat or cold packs, and gradual return to activity. Analgesics such as acetaminophen or nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) relieve pain and inflammation; short courses of muscle relaxants may help with severe spasm. Physical therapy is central to recovery, focusing on core strengthening, flexibility, posture correction, and ergonomic education to prevent recurrence. For radicular pain due to nerve root compression, short courses of oral corticosteroids or epidural steroid injections may reduce inflammation and pain. Chronic or refractory cases may benefit from multidisciplinary pain management including cognitive behavioral therapy, graded exercise programs, and interventional procedures (nerve blocks, radiofrequency ablation). Surgical options (discectomy, laminectomy, spinal fusion) are reserved for structural causes with persistent neurological deficits or intractable pain despite

conservative therapy. Prevention includes weight management, regular exercise, proper lifting techniques, and workplace ergonomics.

title: Bipolar Disorder
text:
# Bipolar Disorder

**Symptoms** Bipolar disorder is characterized by mood episodes that alternate between mania or hypomania and depression. Manic episodes involve abnormally elevated or irritable mood, increased energy, decreased need for sleep, grandiosity, pressured speech, racing thoughts, impulsive or risky behaviors, and impaired judgment; severe mania can include psychosis. Hypomania is a milder form that does not cause marked impairment. Depressive episodes feature persistent low mood, loss of interest, fatigue, changes in appetite or sleep, feelings of worthlessness, and suicidal ideation. The pattern and frequency of episodes vary: some patients have long periods of euthymia, while others experience rapid cycling. Bipolar disorder often begins in late adolescence or early adulthood and can significantly impair social and occupational functioning.

**Treatment** Treatment aims to stabilize mood, prevent relapse, and manage acute episodes. Mood stabilizers such as lithium remain a cornerstone for long-term maintenance and reduce suicide risk; therapeutic monitoring of blood levels and renal/thyroid function is required. Anticonvulsants (valproate, carbamazepine, lamotrigine) are used as mood stabilizers, particularly for rapid cycling or mixed features. Atypical antipsychotics (quetiapine, olanzapine, risperidone) are effective for acute mania and as maintenance therapy. For acute mania, hospitalization may be necessary for safety and stabilization. Depressive episodes are treated cautiously; some antidepressants can trigger mania and are usually combined with a mood stabilizer. Psychotherapy (psychoeducation, family therapy, CBT) supports medication adherence, early recognition of relapse signs, and coping strategies. Lifestyle measures—regular sleep, routine, stress management, and substance avoidance—are important. Long-term follow-up and coordination with mental health services are essential.

title: Bladder Infections (Cystitis / Urinary Tract Infection)
text:
# Bladder Infections (Cystitis / Urinary Tract Infection)

**Symptoms** Bladder infections typically present with urinary urgency, frequency, dysuria (painful or burning urination), suprapubic discomfort, and sometimes hematuria (blood in urine). In uncomplicated lower urinary tract infections, systemic symptoms are usually absent; fever and flank pain suggest upper tract involvement (pyelonephritis). Elderly patients may present atypically with confusion, falls, or generalized weakness. Recurrent infections are common in some populations and may indicate anatomic abnormalities, incomplete bladder emptying, or other risk factors such as catheter use or diabetes.

**Treatment** Uncomplicated cystitis is commonly treated with short courses of oral antibiotics guided by local resistance patterns (e.g., nitrofurantoin,

trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole, fosfomycin). Symptomatic relief with analgesics (phenazopyridine for short term) and increased fluid intake is helpful. For recurrent UTIs, evaluation for predisposing factors is recommended; prophylactic strategies include behavioral measures (urinating after intercourse, hydration), topical vaginal estrogen for postmenopausal women, or low-dose prophylactic antibiotics in selected cases. Complicated UTIs, pyelonephritis, or infections in pregnant women require broader antibiotic coverage and sometimes hospitalization for intravenous therapy. Catheter-associated infections require catheter management and targeted antibiotics. Culture and sensitivity testing guide therapy in recurrent or complicated cases.

title: Blood Pressure (Hypertension)
text:
# Blood Pressure (Hypertension)

**Symptoms** Hypertension is often asymptomatic and is frequently detected during routine screening. When symptoms occur, they are nonspecific: headaches (especially occipital), dizziness, visual disturbances, or palpitations. Severe or malignant hypertension can present with chest pain, shortness of breath, neurological deficits, or signs of end-organ damage (retinopathy, renal impairment). Long-standing uncontrolled hypertension increases the risk of heart disease, stroke, kidney failure, and peripheral vascular disease.

**Treatment** Management combines lifestyle modification and pharmacotherapy. Lifestyle measures include dietary sodium reduction, the DASH diet (rich in fruits, vegetables, low-fat dairy), weight loss, regular aerobic exercise, moderation of alcohol intake, and smoking cessation. First-line antihypertensive drug classes include thiazide diuretics, ACE inhibitors, angiotensin receptor blockers (ARBs), calcium channel blockers, and beta-blockers (in selected patients). Choice of agent depends on comorbidities (diabetes, chronic kidney disease, heart failure), age, and race. Treatment goals are individualized but generally aim for sustained blood pressure control to reduce cardiovascular risk. Regular monitoring, adherence support, and management of secondary causes (renal artery stenosis, endocrine disorders) are part of comprehensive care. In hypertensive emergencies with acute end-organ damage, immediate hospitalization and controlled blood pressure reduction with intravenous agents are required.

title: Bone Fractures
text:
# Bone Fractures

**Symptoms** A fracture typically presents with acute localized pain, swelling, deformity, bruising, and inability to bear weight or use the affected limb. Crepitus or abnormal mobility may be present. Open fractures involve skin disruption and carry infection risk. Certain fractures (hip, vertebral) may present with more subtle symptoms in elderly patients, such as inability to walk or back pain with height loss. Neurovascular compromise (numbness, absent pulses) indicates urgent evaluation.

**Treatment** Initial management follows trauma principles: immobilization, pain control, and assessment for neurovascular injury. Closed fractures are often managed with reduction (realignment) and immobilization using casts or splints. Some fractures require surgical fixation with plates, screws, intramedullary nails, or external fixation to restore alignment and allow early mobilization. Vertebral compression fractures may be treated conservatively with analgesia and bracing; vertebroplasty or kyphoplasty are options in select cases. Open fractures require urgent irrigation, debridement, and antibiotics to prevent infection. Rehabilitation with physiotherapy is essential to restore function and strength. Prevention strategies include fall risk assessment, bone health optimization (calcium, vitamin D, bisphosphonates for osteoporosis), and safety measures.

title: Breast Cancer
text:
# Breast Cancer

**Symptoms** Breast cancer commonly presents as a new, painless lump in the breast or axilla, but symptoms vary: skin changes (dimpling, peau d'orange), nipple retraction, nipple discharge (especially bloody), or localized pain. Advanced disease may cause systemic symptoms such as weight loss, bone pain, or respiratory symptoms from metastases. Screening mammography detects many asymptomatic cancers at an earlier stage. Risk factors include age, family history, genetic mutations (BRCA1/2), hormonal factors, and certain lifestyle elements.

**Treatment** Treatment is multimodal and tailored to tumor stage, receptor status (ER/PR/HER2), and patient factors. Local therapy includes breast-conserving surgery (lumpectomy) with sentinel lymph node biopsy or mastectomy, often followed by radiation therapy for local control. Systemic therapy includes endocrine therapy for hormone receptor–positive tumors (tamoxifen, aromatase inhibitors), chemotherapy for high-risk or triple-negative cancers, and targeted agents for HER2-positive disease (trastuzumab, pertuzumab). Neoadjuvant therapy may shrink tumors preoperatively. Supportive care addresses lymphedema prevention, psychosocial needs, and survivorship issues. Multidisciplinary care involving surgical, medical, and radiation oncology optimizes outcomes. Genetic counseling is recommended for patients with strong family histories or early-onset disease.

title: Bronchitis (Acute and Chronic)
text:
# Bronchitis (Acute and Chronic)

**Symptoms** Acute bronchitis typically follows an upper respiratory infection and presents with cough (initially dry, later productive), chest discomfort, wheeze, and sometimes low-grade fever. Symptoms usually last several weeks. Chronic bronchitis, a form of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), is defined by productive cough for at least three months in two consecutive years and is associated with smoking. Chronic bronchitis leads to persistent cough, sputum production, recurrent infections, and progressive airflow limitation.

**Treatment** Acute bronchitis is usually viral and managed with symptomatic care: hydration, rest, antitussives for severe cough, and bronchodilators for wheeze. Antibiotics are not routinely indicated unless bacterial infection is suspected or in patients with chronic lung disease. For chronic bronchitis, smoking cessation is the most important intervention to slow disease progression. Bronchodilators (short- and long-acting beta-agonists, anticholinergics) and inhaled corticosteroids for selected patients improve symptoms and reduce exacerbations. Pulmonary rehabilitation, vaccination (influenza, pneumococcal), and oxygen therapy for advanced disease are part of comprehensive care. Management of acute exacerbations may require antibiotics, systemic corticosteroids, and hospitalization if severe.

title: Burns
text:
# Burns

**Symptoms** Burn injuries vary by depth and extent. Superficial (first-degree) burns cause erythema and pain without blistering. Partial-thickness (second-degree) burns produce blisters, intense pain, and moist appearance. Full-thickness (third-degree) burns destroy skin layers, may appear white or charred, and can be painless due to nerve destruction. Large or deep burns risk fluid loss, hypothermia, infection, and systemic inflammatory response. Inhalation injury from smoke can cause airway compromise and respiratory failure. Burn severity is assessed by depth and percentage of total body surface area (TBSA) involved.

**Treatment** Initial care follows ABCs (airway, breathing, circulation). For significant burns, fluid resuscitation using formulas (Parkland) prevents hypovolemia. Pain control, wound care (cleansing, debridement), and topical antimicrobials reduce infection risk. Superficial burns heal with conservative care; deeper burns may require surgical excision and skin grafting. Tetanus prophylaxis and early nutritional support are important. Severe burns are best managed in specialized burn centers with multidisciplinary teams addressing wound care, infection control, rehabilitation, and psychological support. Prevention of contractures and long-term scar management (pressure garments, laser therapy) are part of recovery.

title: Bulimia Nervosa
text:
# Bulimia Nervosa

**Symptoms** Bulimia nervosa is an eating disorder characterized by recurrent episodes of binge eating followed by compensatory behaviors to prevent weight gain, such as self-induced vomiting, laxative or diuretic misuse, fasting, or excessive exercise. Patients often maintain a normal weight, making the disorder less obvious. Medical complications include electrolyte disturbances (hypokalemia, hyponatremia), dehydration, dental erosion, esophagitis, gastrointestinal problems, and cardiac arrhythmias. Psychological features include shame, secrecy, and comorbid mood or anxiety disorders.

**Treatment** Treatment combines psychotherapy, nutritional rehabilitation, and medical monitoring. Cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) is the first-line psychotherapeutic approach and focuses on interrupting the binge-purge cycle and addressing distorted body image. Interpersonal therapy and family-based approaches may also help. Pharmacotherapy with SSRIs (fluoxetine) can reduce binge frequency and treat comorbid depression or anxiety. Medical management addresses electrolyte imbalances and complications; hospitalization may be necessary for severe electrolyte disturbances or cardiac risk. Long-term follow-up and relapse prevention strategies are essential.

title: Brain Tumors
text:
# Brain Tumors

**Symptoms** Symptoms of brain tumors depend on tumor location, size, and growth rate. Common presentations include persistent headaches (often worse in the morning), seizures, focal neurological deficits (weakness, sensory loss, speech or vision changes), cognitive or personality changes, nausea, and vomiting. Increased intracranial pressure can cause progressive headache, papilledema, and altered consciousness. Some tumors produce endocrine disturbances if they involve the pituitary region. Symptoms may be subtle and progress gradually, leading to delayed diagnosis.

**Treatment** Management is multidisciplinary and tailored to tumor type (primary vs metastatic), histology, location, and patient factors. Surgical resection is often the first step to obtain tissue diagnosis and reduce mass effect; the extent of resection balances tumor removal with preservation of neurological function. Radiation therapy (conventional or stereotactic radiosurgery) treats residual disease or inoperable tumors. Chemotherapy is used for certain tumor types (glioblastoma, medulloblastoma) and targeted therapies are emerging for tumors with specific molecular markers. Supportive care includes anticonvulsants for seizure control, corticosteroids to reduce edema, and rehabilitation for functional deficits. For metastatic brain disease, systemic cancer control and local therapies (surgery, radiosurgery) are coordinated with oncology. Prognosis varies widely by tumor type and stage.

title: Cancer
text:
# Cancer

**Symptoms** Cancer is not a single disease but a group of disorders characterized by uncontrolled cell growth; symptoms vary widely by cancer type and stage. Common early signs can be subtle and nonspecific: unexplained weight loss, persistent fatigue, night sweats, and low-grade fevers. Local symptoms depend on the organ involved — for example, a lung tumor may cause a persistent cough, hemoptysis (coughing blood), or breathlessness; a colorectal tumor may cause changes in bowel habits, rectal bleeding, or abdominal pain; a breast tumor may present as a new lump, nipple

discharge, or skin changes. Advanced disease often produces systemic symptoms such as cachexia (wasting), bone pain from metastases, neurological deficits from brain involvement, or jaundice from liver metastases. Because early symptoms can mimic benign conditions, persistent or progressive signs warrant medical evaluation.

**Treatment** Cancer treatment is individualized and often multimodal, combining local and systemic therapies. Local control is achieved with surgery to remove tumors when feasible and radiation therapy to eradicate residual disease or palliate symptoms. Systemic therapies include chemotherapy, which uses cytotoxic agents to target rapidly dividing cells; targeted therapies that inhibit specific molecular pathways driving tumor growth (e.g., tyrosine kinase inhibitors); hormonal therapies for hormone-sensitive cancers (breast, prostate); and immunotherapies that harness the immune system to attack cancer cells (checkpoint inhibitors, CAR-T in select settings). Treatment selection depends on tumor histology, stage, molecular markers, patient performance status, and goals of care. Supportive care addresses pain control, management of treatment side effects (nausea, neutropenia, mucositis), nutritional support, and psychosocial needs. Palliative care is integrated early for symptom relief and quality-of-life optimization. Long-term follow-up includes surveillance for recurrence and management of late effects of therapy.

**Cataracts**

**Symptoms** Cataracts are an opacity of the eye’s crystalline lens that develops gradually, most commonly with aging. Early symptoms include blurred or cloudy vision, increased glare or halos around lights (especially at night), difficulty reading small print, faded or yellowed colors, and the need for more light to see clearly. Patients may notice frequent changes in eyeglass prescription or improved near vision (a temporary “second sight” effect) as the lens changes. When cataracts progress, they significantly impair daily activities such as driving and reading and increase fall risk in older adults.

**Treatment** The only definitive treatment for visually significant cataracts is surgical removal of the cloudy lens and implantation of an artificial intraocular lens (IOL). Cataract surgery is one of the most common and successful procedures worldwide and is typically performed on an outpatient basis under local anesthesia. Preoperative assessment includes visual acuity testing, slit-lamp examination, and biometry to select the appropriate IOL power. For patients with mild cataracts, initial management focuses on optimizing lighting, using magnification aids, and updating eyeglass prescriptions. Surgery is recommended when visual impairment affects quality of life or safety. Postoperative care includes topical antibiotics and anti-inflammatory drops, activity modifications for a short period, and follow-up to monitor healing and visual outcomes.

**Celiac Disease**

**Symptoms** Celiac disease is an immune-mediated enteropathy triggered by gluten ingestion in genetically susceptible individuals. Classic symptoms include chronic diarrhea, steatorrhea (fatty stools), abdominal pain, bloating, and weight loss due to malabsorption. Nonclassic or extraintestinal presentations are common and include iron-deficiency anemia, fatigue, osteoporosis from calcium and vitamin D malabsorption, dermatitis herpetiformis (itchy blistering skin rash), neurologic symptoms (peripheral neuropathy, ataxia), and reproductive issues (infertility, recurrent miscarriage). Some patients have minimal gastrointestinal complaints but present with subtle signs such as short stature in children or unexplained elevated liver enzymes.

**Treatment** The cornerstone of treatment is a strict, lifelong gluten-free diet, eliminating wheat, barley, and rye to allow intestinal healing and prevent complications. Dietary adherence typically leads to symptom resolution and mucosal recovery over months to years; nutritional deficiencies (iron, folate, B12, vitamin D) should be identified and corrected. Patients benefit from dietitian support for label reading, cross-contamination avoidance, and balanced nutrition. In refractory cases or when symptoms persist despite a gluten-free diet, evaluation for inadvertent gluten exposure, alternative diagnoses, or refractory celiac disease is necessary; immunosuppressive therapies (e.g., corticosteroids) may be used in severe refractory disease. Regular follow-up includes symptom assessment, serologic testing for antibodies, and monitoring for complications such as osteoporosis and associated autoimmune conditions.

title: Cerebral Palsy
text:
# Cerebral Palsy

**Symptoms** Cerebral palsy (CP) is a group of permanent movement and posture disorders caused by nonprogressive disturbances in the developing fetal or infant brain. Symptoms vary widely in type and severity: spasticity (stiff, tight muscles), dyskinesia (involuntary movements), ataxia (poor coordination), or mixed patterns. Motor impairments lead to delayed milestones, abnormal gait, difficulty with fine motor tasks, and impaired balance. Associated problems commonly include intellectual disability, speech and language difficulties, visual or hearing impairments, epilepsy, and feeding/swallowing problems. The clinical picture is established in early childhood but the functional impact persists lifelong.

**Treatment** There is no cure for CP, but early, multidisciplinary interventions maximize function and quality of life. Physical therapy focuses on stretching, strengthening, gait training, and use of orthoses to improve mobility and prevent contractures. Occupational therapy enhances fine motor skills and adaptive strategies for daily living. Speech and language therapy addresses communication and swallowing. Pharmacologic treatments reduce spasticity and pain: oral agents (baclofen, tizanidine), botulinum toxin injections for focal spasticity, and intrathecal baclofen pumps for severe generalized spasticity. Orthopedic surgeries (tendon lengthening, osteotomies) correct deformities and improve function in selected patients.

Management of seizures, nutritional support, assistive devices (wheelchairs, communication aids), and educational and social support are integral. Lifelong care planning and transition to adult services are important for long-term outcomes.

title: Chickenpox (Varicella)
text:
# Chickenpox (Varicella)

**Symptoms** Chickenpox, caused by varicella-zoster virus, typically presents with a prodrome of fever, malaise, and headache followed by a characteristic pruritic vesicular rash. Lesions appear in successive crops and are found on the trunk, face, and scalp, often spreading to the extremities; lesions progress from macules to papules to vesicles and then crust over. The rash is intensely itchy and may be more severe in adolescents and adults than in children. Complications include bacterial superinfection of lesions, pneumonia (particularly in adults and immunocompromised patients), encephalitis, and, rarely, hemorrhagic varicella.

**Treatment** Management is largely supportive for healthy children: antipyretics (acetaminophen), skin care to reduce scratching (cool baths, calamine lotion), and antihistamines for pruritus. Aspirin should be avoided in children due to the risk of Reye syndrome. Antiviral therapy with acyclovir is recommended for adolescents, adults, pregnant women, and immunocompromised patients to reduce severity and complications; it is most effective when started within 24–48 hours of rash onset. Varicella vaccination is the primary preventive measure and has dramatically reduced disease incidence and complications; post-exposure prophylaxis with varicella vaccine or varicella-zoster immune globulin is considered for high-risk contacts. Hospitalization is required for severe complications such as varicella pneumonia or encephalitis.

title: Cholesterol (Hyperlipidemia)
text:
# Cholesterol (Hyperlipidemia)

**Symptoms** High cholesterol itself is usually asymptomatic and is typically detected through routine blood tests measuring lipid profiles (total cholesterol, LDL, HDL, triglycerides). Symptoms arise from complications of long-standing hyperlipidemia: atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease manifests as chest pain (angina), myocardial infarction, transient ischemic attacks or stroke, and peripheral arterial disease causing claudication. Physical signs of severe lipid disorders may include xanthomas (cholesterol deposits in skin or tendons) and corneal arcus in younger patients.

**Treatment** Management aims to reduce cardiovascular risk through lifestyle modification and pharmacotherapy when indicated. Lifestyle measures include a heart-healthy diet (reduced saturated and trans fats, increased fiber), regular aerobic exercise, weight loss, smoking cessation, and moderation of alcohol. First-line pharmacologic therapy for elevated LDL cholesterol is statins, which reduce cholesterol synthesis and lower cardiovascular events; dosing is based on baseline risk and treatment goals. For patients intolerant to statins or requiring additional LDL lowering, ezetimibe, PCSK9 inhibitors, or bile acid sequestrants may be used. Management of

hypertriglyceridemia includes addressing secondary causes (alcohol, uncontrolled diabetes), fibrates, omega-3 fatty acids, and lifestyle changes. Regular monitoring of lipid levels, liver function tests when on therapy, and individualized risk assessment guide treatment intensity.

title: Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease (COPD)
text:
# Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease (COPD)

**Symptoms** COPD is a progressive respiratory disease characterized by persistent airflow limitation, most commonly caused by long-term exposure to noxious particles such as cigarette smoke. Symptoms include chronic productive cough, dyspnea on exertion that progressively worsens, wheeze, and frequent respiratory infections. Exacerbations—acute worsening of respiratory symptoms—lead to increased morbidity and may require hospitalization. Advanced disease can cause hypoxemia, hypercapnia, pulmonary hypertension, and right heart failure (cor pulmonale).

**Treatment** Management includes smoking cessation as the single most effective intervention to slow disease progression. Pharmacologic therapy uses bronchodilators (short- and long-acting beta-agonists and anticholinergics) to relieve symptoms and reduce exacerbations; inhaled corticosteroids are added for patients with frequent exacerbations and significant eosinophilic inflammation. Pulmonary rehabilitation improves exercise tolerance and quality of life. Long-term oxygen therapy is indicated for patients with chronic hypoxemia to improve survival. Vaccinations (influenza, pneumococcal) reduce infection risk. Acute exacerbations are treated with short courses of systemic corticosteroids, antibiotics when bacterial infection is suspected, and increased bronchodilator therapy; severe exacerbations may require noninvasive ventilation or ICU care. End-of-life planning and palliative care are important for advanced COPD.

title: Cirrhosis
text:
# Cirrhosis

**Symptoms** Cirrhosis is the end stage of chronic liver disease characterized by fibrosis and regenerative nodules that impair hepatic function and portal blood flow. Early symptoms may be nonspecific—fatigue, anorexia, weight loss—but progressive disease leads to jaundice, pruritus, easy bruising, spider angiomas, palmar erythema, and muscle wasting. Portal hypertension causes splenomegaly, ascites (abdominal fluid accumulation), and variceal bleeding. Hepatic encephalopathy presents with confusion, asterixis, and altered consciousness. Complications include spontaneous bacterial peritonitis, hepatorenal syndrome, and hepatocellular carcinoma.

**Treatment** Treatment focuses on managing the underlying cause, preventing and treating complications, and assessing for liver transplantation in eligible patients. Etiology-specific measures include antiviral therapy for viral hepatitis, abstinence and treatment for alcohol-related liver disease, and metabolic control for nonalcoholic fatty liver disease. Management of portal hypertension and ascites includes sodium

restriction, diuretics (spironolactone, furosemide), large-volume paracentesis for tense ascites, and nonselective beta-blockers or endoscopic variceal ligation to prevent variceal bleeding. Hepatic encephalopathy is treated with lactulose and rifaximin to reduce ammonia levels. Surveillance for hepatocellular carcinoma with ultrasound and alpha-fetoprotein is recommended in cirrhotic patients. Advanced liver failure may require referral for transplantation; supportive care and management of complications are essential while awaiting definitive therapy.

title: Common Cold (Viral Upper Respiratory Infection)
text:
# Common Cold (Viral Upper Respiratory Infection)

**Symptoms** The common cold is an acute, self-limited viral infection of the upper respiratory tract, most often caused by rhinoviruses, coronaviruses, and other respiratory viruses. Symptoms typically begin with nasal congestion, rhinorrhea (runny nose), sneezing, sore throat, and mild cough. Fever is uncommon in adults but may occur in children. Symptoms usually peak within 2–3 days and resolve within 7–10 days, though cough can persist longer. Complications include secondary bacterial sinusitis, otitis media (especially in children), and exacerbation of asthma or COPD.

**Treatment** Treatment is symptomatic and supportive. Rest, adequate hydration, saline nasal irrigation, and humidification relieve nasal symptoms. Analgesics and antipyretics (acetaminophen, NSAIDs) manage fever and myalgias. Decongestants and intranasal corticosteroids may provide short-term relief for nasal congestion; antihistamines can reduce rhinorrhea in some patients. Antibiotics are not indicated for uncomplicated viral colds and should be reserved for confirmed bacterial complications. Preventive measures include hand hygiene, respiratory etiquette, and avoiding close contact with infected individuals. For high-risk patients, prompt evaluation is warranted if symptoms worsen or systemic signs develop.

title: COVID-19 (SARS-CoV-2 Infection)
text:
# COVID-19 (SARS-CoV-2 Infection)

**Symptoms** COVID-19 presents with a wide spectrum of illness, from asymptomatic infection to severe respiratory failure and multisystem organ dysfunction. Common symptoms include fever, cough, fatigue, myalgias, sore throat, anosmia (loss of smell), ageusia (loss of taste), nasal congestion, and headache. Gastrointestinal symptoms (nausea, vomiting, diarrhea) occur in some patients. Severe disease is characterized by dyspnea, hypoxemia, pneumonia, acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS), thromboembolic events, and multi-organ failure. Long COVID refers to persistent symptoms—fatigue, cognitive impairment, dyspnea, and others—that continue for weeks to months after acute infection.

**Treatment** Management depends on disease severity. Mild cases are managed at home with supportive care: rest, hydration, antipyretics, and monitoring for worsening symptoms. Antiviral therapy (e.g., oral antivirals or remdesivir in hospitalized patients) is indicated for high-risk individuals early in the disease course to reduce progression. For

patients requiring oxygen or hospitalization, corticosteroids (dexamethasone) reduce mortality in those with hypoxemia; anticoagulation is used to prevent thrombotic complications. Monoclonal antibodies and other targeted therapies have been used for early treatment in high-risk patients, though effectiveness depends on circulating variants. Severe cases may require advanced respiratory support (high-flow oxygen, noninvasive ventilation, mechanical ventilation) and critical care management. Vaccination remains the primary prevention strategy, significantly reducing severe disease, hospitalization, and death. Rehabilitation and multidisciplinary care address long COVID symptoms.

title: Diabetes (Type 1 and Type 2)
text:
# Diabetes (Type 1 and Type 2)

**Symptoms** Diabetes mellitus presents with polyuria (frequent urination), polydipsia (excessive thirst), polyphagia (increased hunger), unexplained weight loss (more common in type 1), fatigue, blurred vision, and slow wound healing. Type 1 diabetes often has abrupt onset in children or young adults and may present with diabetic ketoacidosis (nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, rapid breathing). Type 2 diabetes develops gradually and is associated with insulin resistance, obesity, and metabolic syndrome; many patients are asymptomatic early and are diagnosed on screening. Chronic hyperglycemia leads to microvascular complications (retinopathy, nephropathy, neuropathy) and macrovascular disease (coronary artery disease, stroke, peripheral arterial disease).

**Treatment** Management includes lifestyle modification (dietary changes, weight loss, regular physical activity) and pharmacotherapy. Type 1 diabetes requires lifelong insulin therapy delivered by injections or insulin pump, with education on carbohydrate counting, glucose monitoring, and hypoglycemia management. Type 2 diabetes treatment begins with lifestyle measures and metformin; additional agents (SGLT2 inhibitors, GLP-1 receptor agonists, DPP-4 inhibitors, sulfonylureas, insulin) are added based on glycemic control, comorbidities, and cardiovascular/renal benefits. Regular monitoring of HbA1c, self-monitoring of blood glucose, screening for complications, blood pressure and lipid control, and vaccination are essential. Patient education, multidisciplinary care, and individualized targets improve outcomes.

title: Depression (Major Depressive Disorder)
text:
# Depression (Major Depressive Disorder)

**Symptoms** Major depressive disorder is characterized by persistent low mood, loss of interest or pleasure (anhedonia), changes in appetite or weight, sleep disturbances (insomnia or hypersomnia), psychomotor changes, fatigue, feelings of worthlessness or excessive guilt, diminished concentration, and recurrent thoughts of death or suicide. Symptoms must persist for at least two weeks and cause significant impairment. Depression often coexists with anxiety, substance use, and chronic medical conditions, complicating diagnosis and treatment.

**Treatment** Treatment combines psychotherapy and pharmacotherapy. First-line psychotherapies include cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) and interpersonal therapy (IPT). Antidepressant medications—SSRIs, SNRIs, atypical antidepressants, tricyclics, and MAO inhibitors—are chosen based on side-effect profiles, comorbidities, and prior response. For severe or treatment-resistant depression, augmentation strategies, electroconvulsive therapy (ECT), or newer neuromodulation techniques (TMS, vagus nerve stimulation) may be used. Safety planning and suicide risk assessment are critical. Long-term maintenance therapy reduces relapse risk; lifestyle measures, social support, and treatment of comorbid conditions are important.

title: Dementia (including Alzheimer's and Vascular Dementia)
text:
# Dementia (including Alzheimer's and Vascular Dementia)

**Symptoms** Dementia is a syndrome of progressive cognitive decline affecting memory, language, executive function, and daily living activities. Alzheimer's disease typically begins with short-term memory loss and progresses to impair multiple cognitive domains; vascular dementia often has a stepwise decline with focal neurological signs. Behavioral and psychiatric symptoms—apathy, agitation, psychosis, sleep disturbance—are common and distressing for caregivers. Functional decline leads to dependence and increased care needs.

**Treatment** Management includes symptomatic pharmacotherapy (cholinesterase inhibitors for mild-moderate Alzheimer's; memantine for moderate-severe disease) and nonpharmacologic interventions (cognitive stimulation, structured routines, environmental modifications). Treating vascular risk factors (hypertension, diabetes, hyperlipidemia) can slow progression in vascular dementia. Behavioral symptoms are first addressed with nonpharmacologic strategies; antipsychotics are used cautiously for severe agitation due to increased mortality risk. Caregiver support, advanced care planning, and multidisciplinary coordination are essential.

title: Dermatitis (Eczema, Contact Dermatitis, Atopic Dermatitis)
text:
# Dermatitis (Eczema, Contact Dermatitis, Atopic Dermatitis)

**Symptoms** Dermatitis presents with erythema, pruritus (itching), scaling, vesicles, and sometimes oozing or crusting. Atopic dermatitis often begins in childhood with flexural involvement and intense itch; contact dermatitis results from exposure to irritants or allergens and follows a distribution corresponding to exposure. Chronic dermatitis leads to lichenification (thickened skin) and secondary infection.

**Treatment** Treatment focuses on trigger avoidance, skin hydration with emollients, and anti-inflammatory therapy. Topical corticosteroids are first-line for flares; topical calcineurin inhibitors are alternatives for sensitive areas. For severe or widespread disease, short courses of systemic corticosteroids or immunosuppressants (methotrexate, cyclosporine) may be used; newer biologics (dupilumab) are effective for moderate-severe atopic dermatitis. Antihistamines relieve itch; antibiotics treat

secondary bacterial infection. Patient education on gentle skin care and avoidance of irritants is key.

title: Diarrhea (Acute and Chronic)
text:
# Diarrhea (Acute and Chronic)

**Symptoms** Diarrhea is increased stool frequency and/or liquidity. Acute infectious diarrhea often presents with abdominal cramps, fever, nausea, and sometimes bloody stools. Chronic diarrhea (lasting >4 weeks) may be due to inflammatory bowel disease, irritable bowel syndrome, malabsorption (celiac disease, pancreatic insufficiency), microscopic colitis, or medication side effects. Dehydration, electrolyte disturbances, and weight loss are important complications.

**Treatment** Acute infectious diarrhea is managed with rehydration (oral rehydration solutions), symptomatic care, and targeted antibiotics for specific bacterial pathogens or severe cases. Antimotility agents (loperamide) can be used in selected nonbloody cases. Chronic diarrhea requires evaluation to identify the cause (stool studies, blood tests, endoscopy, imaging) and disease-specific therapy: anti-inflammatories and immunosuppressants for IBD, gluten-free diet for celiac disease, pancreatic enzyme replacement for pancreatic insufficiency, bile acid sequestrants for bile acid diarrhea, and dietary modifications for IBS. Nutritional support and correction of electrolyte imbalances are essential.

title: Digestive Disorders (GERD, IBS, Peptic Ulcer Disease)
text:
# Digestive Disorders (GERD, IBS, Peptic Ulcer Disease)

**Symptoms** Gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD) causes heartburn, regurgitation, and sometimes chronic cough or laryngitis. Irritable bowel syndrome (IBS) presents with abdominal pain associated with altered bowel habits (constipation, diarrhea, or mixed) and bloating. Peptic ulcer disease causes epigastric pain, often related to meals, and may present with bleeding or perforation in complications.

**Treatment** GERD management includes lifestyle measures (weight loss, head-of-bed elevation, avoiding trigger foods) and acid suppression with proton pump inhibitors (PPIs) or H2 blockers; refractory cases may need surgical fundoplication. IBS treatment is symptom-directed: dietary changes (low FODMAP), fiber, antispasmodics, laxatives or antidiarrheals, and psychological therapies (CBT). Peptic ulcer disease treatment targets Helicobacter pylori eradication when present (combination antibiotics plus PPI) and acid suppression; avoid NSAIDs or use protective strategies if NSAIDs are necessary.

title: Down Syndrome (Trisomy 21)
text:
# Down Syndrome (Trisomy 21)

**Symptoms** Down syndrome is a genetic condition with characteristic facial features, intellectual disability of variable severity, hypotonia, and congenital anomalies (especially cardiac defects such as atrioventricular septal defects). Other issues

include thyroid dysfunction, hearing and vision problems, gastrointestinal malformations, and increased risk of leukemia and early-onset Alzheimer’s disease.

**Treatment** Care is multidisciplinary and lifelong. Early intervention with developmental therapies (physical, occupational, speech) improves outcomes. Cardiac defects often require surgical correction in infancy. Regular screening for thyroid disease, hearing and vision problems, celiac disease, and hematologic abnormalities is recommended. Educational support, social services, and transition planning to adult care are important. Management focuses on maximizing independence and quality of life.

title: Drug Abuse (Prescription and Illicit Substances)
text:
# Drug Abuse (Prescription and Illicit Substances)

**Symptoms** Drug abuse manifests with behavioral changes (neglect of responsibilities, social withdrawal), physical signs (weight loss, track marks, nasal septum damage), cognitive impairment, mood instability, and tolerance/withdrawal phenomena. Specific substances produce characteristic effects: stimulants cause agitation and insomnia; opioids cause sedation and respiratory depression; benzodiazepines cause sedation and memory impairment.

**Treatment** Treatment includes medical stabilization, detoxification, pharmacotherapy for specific dependencies (buprenorphine/methadone for opioids, benzodiazepine tapering for sedative dependence), and psychosocial interventions (CBT, contingency management). Harm-reduction strategies (needle exchange, naloxone distribution) reduce morbidity and mortality. Long-term recovery involves relapse prevention, social support, vocational rehabilitation, and treatment of co-occurring mental health disorders.

title: Diphtheria (rare in vaccinated populations)
text:
# Diphtheria (rare in vaccinated populations)

**Symptoms** Diphtheria, caused by Corynebacterium diphtheriae, presents with sore throat, low-grade fever, and a characteristic gray-white pseudomembrane on the tonsils and pharynx that can cause airway obstruction. Toxin-mediated complications include myocarditis and neuropathies. In countries with high vaccination coverage, diphtheria is rare but remains a risk in unvaccinated populations.

**Treatment** Immediate management includes administration of diphtheria antitoxin to neutralize circulating toxin and prompt antibiotic therapy (penicillin or erythromycin) to eradicate the organism and reduce transmission. Airway management may be necessary for obstruction. Close monitoring for cardiac and neurologic complications is required. Prevention relies on vaccination (DTaP/Tdap) and booster doses per schedule.

title: Epilepsy
text:
# Epilepsy

**Symptoms & Treatment (concise)** Epilepsy causes recurrent unprovoked seizures—transient disturbances of brain function manifesting as convulsions, staring spells, sensory phenomena, or loss of awareness. Diagnosis uses EEG and neuroimaging. Treatment centers on antiseizure medications (valproate, carbamazepine, levetiracetam, lamotrigine) tailored to seizure type; refractory cases may benefit from epilepsy surgery, vagus nerve stimulation, or ketogenic diet. Safety counseling and driving restrictions are important.

Eczema (Atopic Dermatitis)

**Symptoms & Treatment (concise)** Intensely itchy, inflamed skin with chronic relapsing course. Management: emollients, topical corticosteroids, topical calcineurin inhibitors, avoidance of triggers, and systemic therapies or biologics for severe disease.

title: Eating Disorders (Anorexia, Bulimia, Binge Eating)
text:
# Eating Disorders (Anorexia, Bulimia, Binge Eating)

**Symptoms & Treatment (concise)** Disordered eating with medical and psychiatric complications. Treatment is multidisciplinary: nutritional rehabilitation, psychotherapy (CBT, family-based therapy), medical monitoring, and pharmacotherapy for comorbid conditions.

title: Eye Diseases (Glaucoma, Macular Degeneration)
text:
# Eye Diseases (Glaucoma, Macular Degeneration)

**Symptoms & Treatment (concise)** Glaucoma causes progressive peripheral vision loss; treated with topical pressure-lowering agents, laser, or surgery. Age-related macular degeneration causes central vision loss; management includes anti-VEGF injections for wet AMD and lifestyle/nutritional support for dry AMD.

title: Fibromyalgia
text:

**Symptoms & Treatment (concise)** Widespread musculoskeletal pain, fatigue, sleep disturbance. Management: exercise, CBT, sleep hygiene, and medications (duloxetine, pregabalin) for symptom control.

title: Gout
text:
# Gout

**Symptoms & Treatment (concise)** Acute monoarticular arthritis (podagra), intense pain, swelling. Acute treatment: NSAIDs, colchicine, corticosteroids. Long-term: urate-lowering therapy (allopurinol, febuxostat) and lifestyle modification.

text:

**Symptoms & Treatment (concise)** Acute diarrhea, vomiting, abdominal cramps. Rehydration, supportive care; antibiotics for specific bacterial causes.

title: Heart Disease (Ischemic Heart Disease, Coronary Artery Disease)
text:
# Heart Disease (Ischemic Heart Disease, Coronary Artery Disease)

**Symptoms** Ischemic heart disease commonly presents with exertional chest pain (angina), shortness of breath, fatigue, and in acute coronary syndromes with severe chest pain, diaphoresis, nausea, and syncope. Atypical presentations occur in women, elderly, and diabetics. Chronic ischemia leads to heart failure and arrhythmias.

**Treatment** Management includes risk factor modification (smoking cessation, lipid control, blood pressure management, diabetes control), antiplatelet therapy (aspirin), statins, antianginal medications (beta-blockers, nitrates, calcium channel blockers), and revascularization (PCI or CABG) for significant coronary stenosis. Acute MI requires rapid reperfusion (PCI or thrombolysis), antithrombotic therapy, and intensive care. Cardiac rehabilitation improves outcomes.

title: Hepatitis (A, B, C, Autoimmune, Alcoholic)
text:
# Hepatitis (A, B, C, Autoimmune, Alcoholic)

**Symptoms** Viral hepatitis presents with fatigue, anorexia, nausea, right upper quadrant discomfort, jaundice, dark urine, and pale stools. Chronic hepatitis may be asymptomatic until advanced liver disease develops.

**Treatment** Acute viral hepatitis A is supportive; hepatitis B and C have effective antiviral therapies (direct-acting antivirals for HCV; nucleos(t)ide analogues for HBV) to reduce progression to cirrhosis. Vaccination prevents hepatitis A and B. Management of alcoholic hepatitis includes abstinence and supportive care; autoimmune hepatitis requires immunosuppression.

HIV/AIDS (covered in A but expanded for completeness)

**Symptoms & Treatment (concise)** See Section A for detailed management; ART, opportunistic infection prophylaxis, and monitoring are central.

Hypertension (covered in B but expanded here)

**Symptoms & Treatment (concise)** See Section B.

title: Hemorrhoids
text:
# Hemorrhoids

**Symptoms** Rectal bleeding, pain, itching, and prolapse. External hemorrhoids cause perianal pain; internal hemorrhoids may bleed with defecation.

**Treatment** Conservative care: fiber, stool softeners, sitz baths, topical agents. Office procedures (rubber band ligation, sclerotherapy) for persistent symptomatic hemorrhoids; surgical hemorrhoidectomy for severe or recurrent disease.

title: Hernia (Inguinal, Femoral, Ventral)
text:
# Hernia (Inguinal, Femoral, Ventral)

**Symptoms** Bulge in the groin or abdominal wall, discomfort with straining; incarcerated hernia causes severe pain and obstruction.

**Treatment** Elective surgical repair (open or laparoscopic) for symptomatic hernias; urgent surgery for incarceration or strangulation.

title: Thyroid Disorders (Hypothyroidism, Hyperthyroidism)
text:
# Thyroid Disorders (Hypothyroidism, Hyperthyroidism)

**Symptoms** Hypothyroidism: fatigue, weight gain, cold intolerance, constipation, bradycardia. Hyperthyroidism: weight loss, heat intolerance, palpitations, tremor, anxiety.

**Treatment** Hypothyroidism: levothyroxine replacement with dose titration by TSH. Hyperthyroidism: antithyroid drugs (methimazole, propylthiouracil), radioactive iodine ablation, or surgery for definitive treatment; beta-blockers for symptomatic control.

title: Hair Loss (Alopecia Areata, Androgenetic Alopecia)
text:
# Hair Loss (Alopecia Areata, Androgenetic Alopecia)

**Symptoms** Patchy hair loss (alopecia areata) or progressive thinning (androgenetic alopecia). Psychological impact can be significant.

**Treatment** Topical or intralesional corticosteroids for alopecia areata; minoxidil and finasteride for androgenetic alopecia; hair transplantation and cosmetic options for advanced cases.

title: Headaches (Tension, Migraine, Cluster)
text:
# Headaches (Tension, Migraine, Cluster)

**Symptoms** Tension headaches cause bilateral pressure; migraines cause unilateral throbbing pain with photophobia, phonophobia, and sometimes aura; cluster headaches are severe, unilateral, and associated with autonomic features.

**Treatment** Acute migraine: NSAIDs, triptans, antiemetics. Preventive therapy: beta-blockers, antiepileptics, CGRP inhibitors. Tension headaches: analgesics, stress management. Cluster headaches: oxygen therapy, triptans, and preventive verapamil.

title: Hearing Loss
text:
# Hearing Loss

**Symptoms** Gradual or sudden reduction in hearing, tinnitus, difficulty understanding speech. Causes include presbycusis, noise exposure, otitis media, ototoxic drugs.

**Treatment** Evaluation with audiometry; hearing aids, cochlear implants for severe sensorineural loss; medical or surgical treatment for conductive causes (e.g., otosclerosis, chronic otitis media).

title: Migraine
text:
# Migraine

**Symptoms** Recurrent moderate-to-severe headaches, often unilateral and pulsatile, associated with nausea, vomiting, photophobia, and phonophobia; some patients experience aura (visual or sensory disturbances) preceding headache.

**Treatment** Acute therapy: NSAIDs, triptans, antiemetics. Preventive therapy for frequent attacks: beta-blockers, antiepileptics (topiramate), antidepressants (amitriptyline), and CGRP monoclonal antibodies. Lifestyle triggers identification and management, sleep hygiene, and stress reduction are important.

title: Multiple Sclerosis (MS)
text:
# Multiple Sclerosis (MS)

**Symptoms** Demyelinating disease causing sensory disturbances, weakness, visual loss (optic neuritis), ataxia, bladder dysfunction, and cognitive changes. Symptoms often remit and relapse in relapsing-remitting MS.

**Treatment** Acute relapses: high-dose corticosteroids. Disease-modifying therapies (interferons, glatiramer acetate, monoclonal antibodies, oral agents) reduce relapse

rate and slow progression. Symptomatic management (spasticity, fatigue, bladder dysfunction) and multidisciplinary rehabilitation are essential.

title: Malaria
text:
# Malaria

**Symptoms** Fever, chills, sweats, headache, myalgias, and in severe cases anemia, jaundice, cerebral involvement, and multi-organ failure. Travel history to endemic areas is key.

**Treatment** Prompt diagnosis with blood smear or rapid tests. Uncomplicated malaria treated with artemisinin-based combination therapies (ACTs); severe malaria requires intravenous artesunate and supportive care. Prevention includes prophylaxis for travelers and vector control.

title: Mental Health Disorders (General overview)
text:
# Mental Health Disorders (General overview)

**Symptoms & Treatment (concise)** Covers anxiety, depression, psychotic disorders, personality disorders. Treatment: psychotherapy, pharmacotherapy, social support, and crisis intervention when needed.

title: Measles
text:
# Measles

**Symptoms & Treatment (concise)** Fever, cough, coryza, conjunctivitis, Koplik spots, and maculopapular rash. Supportive care; vitamin A reduces morbidity. Vaccination prevents disease.

title: Meningitis
text:
# Meningitis

**Symptoms & Treatment (concise)** Fever, headache, neck stiffness, photophobia, altered mental status. Bacterial meningitis requires urgent empiric IV antibiotics and sometimes adjunctive corticosteroids; viral meningitis is usually supportive care.

title: Muscular Dystrophy
text:
# Muscular Dystrophy

**Symptoms & Treatment (concise)** Progressive muscle weakness, gait disturbance, respiratory compromise in advanced disease. Management: multidisciplinary care, physiotherapy, respiratory support, and genetic counseling; disease-specific therapies emerging for some types.

title: Myopia (Nearsightedness)
text:
# Myopia (Nearsightedness)

**Symptoms & Treatment (concise)** Blurry distance vision; corrected with glasses, contact lenses, or refractive surgery; myopia control strategies (orthokeratology, low-dose atropine) for children.

title: Mouth Ulcers (Aphthous Stomatitis)
text:
# Mouth Ulcers (Aphthous Stomatitis)

**Symptoms & Treatment (concise)** Painful oral ulcers; topical corticosteroids, antiseptic mouthwashes, and addressing nutritional deficiencies help; recurrent cases require evaluation.

title: Menopause
text:
# Menopause

**Symptoms & Treatment (concise)** Vasomotor symptoms (hot flashes), sleep disturbance, mood changes, vaginal dryness, osteoporosis risk. Management: lifestyle measures, hormone replacement therapy (individualized), nonhormonal options for vasomotor symptoms, bone health strategies.

title: Nutrition (Malnutrition, Obesity)
text:
# Nutrition (Malnutrition, Obesity)

**Symptoms & Treatment (concise)** Malnutrition: weight loss, muscle wasting; treat with nutritional rehabilitation and address underlying causes. Obesity: excess weight with metabolic complications; treat with lifestyle, pharmacotherapy, and bariatric surgery when indicated.

title: Neuropathy (Peripheral Neuropathy)
text:
# Neuropathy (Peripheral Neuropathy)

**Symptoms & Treatment (concise)** Numbness, tingling, burning pain, weakness. Treat underlying cause (diabetes, toxins), symptomatic pain control (gabapentin, duloxetine), and rehabilitation.

Nasal Allergies (Allergic Rhinitis)

**Symptoms & Treatment (concise)** Sneezing, rhinorrhea, congestion; treat with intranasal steroids, antihistamines, and immunotherapy.

title: Nephritis (Glomerulonephritis)

**Symptoms & Treatment (concise)** Hematuria, proteinuria, edema, hypertension. Management depends on cause: immunosuppression for immune-mediated disease, blood pressure control, and renal support.

title: Osteoporosis

# Osteoporosis

**Symptoms & Treatment (concise)** Often asymptomatic until fracture; fragility fractures of hip, spine. Treatment: calcium/vitamin D, bisphosphonates, denosumab, lifestyle measures, fall prevention.

title: Oral Health (Dental Caries, Periodontitis)

title: Parkinson's Disease
text:
# Parkinson's Disease

**Symptoms & Treatment (concise)** Bradykinesia, rigidity, resting tremor, postural instability. Treatment: levodopa/carbidopa, dopamine agonists, MAO-B inhibitors, deep brain stimulation for selected patients, and multidisciplinary rehabilitation.

title: Pneumonia
text:
# Pneumonia

**Symptoms & Treatment (concise)** Fever, cough, sputum, dyspnea, chest pain. Diagnosis by chest X-ray; treat with appropriate antibiotics, oxygen, and supportive care; vaccination prevents many cases.

title: Psoriasis
text:
# Psoriasis

title: Prostate Cancer
text:
# Prostate Cancer

**Symptoms & Treatment (concise)** Often asymptomatic early; urinary symptoms or metastatic bone pain in advanced disease. Management: active surveillance, surgery, radiation, androgen deprivation therapy, and systemic agents for advanced disease.

title: Rheumatoid Arthritis
text:
# Rheumatoid Arthritis

**Symptoms & Treatment (concise)** Symmetric inflammatory polyarthritis with morning stiffness. Treat with DMARDs (methotrexate), biologics, NSAIDs, and rehabilitation.

title: Respiratory Infections (Bronchitis, Pneumonia)

# Respiratory Infections (Bronchitis, Pneumonia)

Symptoms & Treatment (concise) See Bronchitis and Pneumonia sections; supportive care and targeted antibiotics when indicated.

Rickets (Vitamin D Deficiency in Children)

Symptoms & Treatment (concise) Bone pain, deformities, delayed growth. Treat with vitamin D and calcium supplementation and address dietary causes.

Rosacea

Symptoms & Treatment (concise) Facial flushing, papules, telangiectasia. Treat with topical metronidazole, azelaic acid, oral antibiotics for inflammatory lesions, and laser for telangiectasia.

Section S — Full expanded content (20 pages; 10 topics)

Stroke (Ischemic and Hemorrhagic)

Symptoms Sudden focal neurological deficits: weakness or numbness on one side, speech disturbance, visual loss, dizziness, severe headache (hemorrhagic). Time-sensitive emergency—“time is brain.”

Treatment Immediate assessment with CT/MRI. Ischemic stroke: reperfusion with IV thrombolysis (if within window) and endovascular thrombectomy for large vessel occlusion; secondary prevention with antiplatelets, anticoagulation for cardioembolic sources, risk factor control, and rehabilitation. Hemorrhagic stroke: blood pressure control, neurosurgical intervention for large bleeds, and reversal of anticoagulation when applicable.

Schizophrenia

Symptoms & Treatment (concise) Psychosis with hallucinations, delusions, disorganized thought, negative symptoms. Antipsychotic medications, psychosocial interventions, and long-term support are central.

Skin Cancer (Melanoma, Basal Cell, Squamous Cell)

Symptoms & Treatment (concise) New or changing skin lesions; biopsy for diagnosis. Surgical excision is primary treatment; advanced melanoma treated with immunotherapy and targeted agents.

Stress (Acute and Chronic)

Symptoms & Treatment (concise) Psychological and somatic symptoms (sleep disturbance, headaches, GI upset). Management: stress reduction techniques, CBT, lifestyle changes, and treatment of comorbid conditions.

Sinusitis

Symptoms & Treatment (concise) Facial pain/pressure, nasal congestion, purulent nasal discharge. Supportive care, intranasal steroids, and antibiotics for bacterial cases.

Stomach Ulcers (Peptic Ulcer Disease)

Symptoms & Treatment (concise) Epigastric pain, dyspepsia, possible bleeding. Treat H. pylori if present, PPI therapy, and avoid NSAIDs.

title: Q Fever
text:
# Q Fever

**Symptoms** Q fever, caused by Coxiella burnetii, presents with fever, severe headache, myalgias, and sometimes atypical pneumonia or hepatitis. Chronic Q fever can cause endocarditis in predisposed individuals.

**Treatment** Acute Q fever is treated with doxycycline; chronic infection (endocarditis) requires prolonged combination therapy (doxycycline plus hydroxychloroquine) and specialist management. Prevention includes occupational precautions for at-risk workers and control of animal reservoirs.

title: Xeroderma and X-linked Disorders
text:
# Xeroderma and X-linked Disorders

**Xeroderma (Xeroderma Pigmentosum) Symptoms** A rare genetic disorder of DNA repair causing extreme sensitivity to UV light, early freckling, pigmentary changes, and a high risk of skin cancers at a young age.

**Treatment** Strict UV protection, regular dermatologic surveillance, early excision of suspicious lesions, and genetic counseling.

**X-linked Disorders (Overview) Symptoms & Treatment (concise)** A group of genetic conditions transmitted via the X chromosome (e.g., hemophilia, Duchenne muscular dystrophy). Management is disease-specific: factor replacement for hemophilia,

multidisciplinary care and emerging gene therapies for muscular dystrophy, and genetic counseling for families.

# Yeast Infections (Candidiasis)

**Symptoms** Vaginal candidiasis: itching, thick white discharge, dysuria. Oropharyngeal candidiasis: white plaques, soreness. Invasive candidiasis: fever, sepsis in immunocompromised patients.

**Treatment** Topical or oral antifungals (fluconazole, topical azoles) for mucocutaneous disease; systemic antifungals (echinocandins, fluconazole) for invasive disease. Address predisposing factors (diabetes, antibiotics, immunosuppression).

title: Yellow Fever

title: Zika Virus

# Zika Virus

**Symptoms** Often mild febrile illness with rash, conjunctivitis, arthralgia; infection during pregnancy can cause congenital Zika syndrome (microcephaly, neurologic defects).
