title: Zinc Deficiency
text:
# Zinc Deficiency

**Symptoms & Treatment (concise)** Growth retardation, impaired wound healing, immune dysfunction. Treat with zinc supplementation and dietary correction.

title: Abdominal Pain
text:
# Abdominal Pain

**Symptoms** Abdominal pain ranges from mild, intermittent cramping to severe, constant pain and may be localized (e.g., right lower quadrant) or diffuse. Associated features that help identify cause include nausea, vomiting, anorexia, fever, bloating, constipation or diarrhea, hematemesis or melena, urinary symptoms, and referred pain to the shoulder or back. Physical exam findings such as guarding, rebound tenderness, rigidity, abdominal distension, absent bowel sounds, or a palpable mass suggest peritonitis, obstruction, or an intra-abdominal process. Red flags requiring urgent evaluation include hypotension, high fever, progressive peritoneal signs, persistent vomiting, or signs of shock. **Treatment** Management is directed at the underlying

diagnosis: urgent surgical consultation and appendectomy for appendicitis; bowel rest, nasogastric decompression, and often surgery for mechanical obstruction; IV fluids, analgesia, and antibiotics for intra-abdominal sepsis; proton pump inhibitors and H. pylori eradication for peptic ulcer disease; and supportive care (oral rehydration, antiemetics) for viral gastroenteritis. Initial ED care emphasizes hemodynamic stabilization, analgesia, targeted imaging (ultrasound, CT), laboratory testing (CBC, electrolytes, liver enzymes, amylase/lipase), and timely specialty referral when indicated.

**Abscess Skin and Internal**

**Symptoms** Superficial skin abscesses present as a painful, erythematous, warm, fluctuant nodule often with surrounding cellulitis; systemic symptoms (fever, malaise) may accompany larger or deeper infections. Internal abscesses (peritonsillar, intra-abdominal, hepatic, pelvic) produce localized pain, fever, leukocytosis, and organ-specific signs such as dysphagia, abdominal tenderness, or jaundice. Chronic or recurrent abscesses raise concern for underlying conditions (diabetes, immunosuppression, foreign body, fistula). **Treatment** Superficial abscesses require incision and drainage as the primary therapy, with wound care and culture when indicated; oral antibiotics are added for systemic signs, extensive cellulitis, immunocompromise, or difficult-to-drain locations. Deep or visceral abscesses usually need image-guided percutaneous drainage or surgical drainage plus targeted intravenous antibiotics guided by culture and sensitivity. Address predisposing factors (glycemic control, removal of foreign bodies) and provide tetanus prophylaxis when appropriate.

**Addison's Disease Primary Adrenal Insufficiency**

**Symptoms** Chronic adrenal insufficiency causes progressive fatigue, anorexia, weight loss, abdominal pain, salt craving, orthostatic dizziness, hyperpigmentation of sun-exposed skin and mucosa, hyponatremia, and hyperkalemia. Acute adrenal crisis presents with severe hypotension, vomiting, abdominal pain, fever, confusion, and can be life-threatening if not treated promptly. Non-specific symptoms often delay diagnosis until biochemical testing reveals low cortisol and elevated ACTH in primary disease. **Treatment** Lifelong replacement therapy with glucocorticoids (hydrocortisone or equivalent) and mineralocorticoid (fludrocortisone) is required for primary Addison's disease, with dose adjustments during stress or illness. Acute adrenal crisis requires immediate IV hydrocortisone, aggressive fluid resuscitation with isotonic saline, correction of electrolytes, and treatment of precipitating causes (infection, trauma). Patient education on sick-day dosing, emergency injectable steroids, and medical alert identification is essential to prevent recurrent crises.

**Aneurysm Abdominal Aortic and Cerebral**

**Symptoms** Many aneurysms are clinically silent until enlargement or rupture. Abdominal aortic aneurysm (AAA) may produce a pulsatile abdominal mass, back or abdominal pain, or a sense of fullness; rupture causes sudden severe abdominal or back pain, hypotension, and shock. Cerebral (berry) aneurysm rupture causes an abrupt, severe “thunderclap” headache, neck stiffness, photophobia, nausea, vomiting, focal neurologic deficits, and decreased consciousness. Unruptured cerebral aneurysms may cause cranial nerve palsies or seizures if large. **Treatment** Management depends on size, location, and rupture risk. Small, asymptomatic AAAs are monitored with serial imaging and aggressive risk-factor modification (blood-pressure control, smoking cessation). Elective repair (endovascular aneurysm repair or open surgery) is recommended when diameter exceeds guideline thresholds or growth is rapid. Ruptured aneurysms require emergency resuscitation and urgent surgical or endovascular repair. For cerebral aneurysms, neurosurgical clipping or endovascular coiling is used based on anatomy and patient factors; blood-pressure control and neurosurgical ICU care are critical after rupture.

title: Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis ALS
text:
# Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis ALS

**Symptoms** ALS is a progressive motor neuron disease causing painless weakness, muscle wasting, fasciculations, spasticity, dysarthria, dysphagia, and eventual respiratory muscle involvement. Symptoms often begin focally (limb or bulbar) and spread, with preserved sensation and autonomic function. Respiratory decline leads to orthopnea, morning headaches, and recurrent pulmonary infections; cognitive or behavioral changes occur in a subset. **Treatment** There is no cure; care is multidisciplinary and focuses on slowing progression, preserving function, and symptom control. Disease-modifying drugs (riluzole, edaravone) may modestly slow decline. Interventions include respiratory support (noninvasive ventilation, cough assist), nutritional support (enteral feeding when needed), physical and occupational therapy to maintain mobility and safety, management of spasticity and secretions, and early palliative care planning. Genetic counseling is offered when familial forms are suspected.

title: Angina Pectoris Stable and Unstable
text:
# Angina Pectoris Stable and Unstable

**Symptoms** Angina presents as chest discomfort, pressure, or tightness precipitated by exertion or emotional stress and relieved by rest or nitrates; radiation to jaw, neck, shoulder, or arm and associated dyspnea, diaphoresis, or nausea may occur. Unstable angina features new-onset, worsening, or rest angina and may herald myocardial infarction. Atypical symptoms are common in women, elderly, and diabetics.

**Treatment** Immediate management of acute ischemia includes oxygen if hypoxic, sublingual nitroglycerin, aspirin, and rapid triage. Long-term therapy focuses on antianginal medications (beta-blockers, nitrates, calcium channel blockers), antiplatelet therapy, high-intensity statin therapy, ACE inhibitors for comorbidities,

smoking cessation, diabetes control, and structured exercise. Revascularization with percutaneous coronary intervention or coronary artery bypass grafting is indicated for refractory symptoms or significant ischemia/anatomic disease.

title: Anaphylaxis Severe Systemic Allergy
text:
# Anaphylaxis Severe Systemic Allergy

**Symptoms** Anaphylaxis is a rapid, life-threatening allergic reaction characterized by sudden onset of urticaria, angioedema, bronchospasm with wheeze and respiratory distress, hypotension, gastrointestinal symptoms (vomiting, diarrhea), and possible loss of consciousness. Onset is typically within minutes to hours after exposure to an allergen (foods, drugs, insect stings). Biphasic reactions can occur hours after initial recovery. **Treatment** Immediate intramuscular epinephrine is the first-line therapy and should not be delayed; secure airway, provide high-flow oxygen, and give aggressive IV fluids for hypotension. Adjunctive treatments include antihistamines and corticosteroids to reduce prolonged or biphasic reactions, bronchodilators for bronchospasm, and observation for at least 4–24 hours depending on severity. Patients require education on avoidance, prescription of epinephrine auto-injectors, and referral to allergy specialists for testing and immunotherapy when appropriate.

title: Aortic Stenosis Valvular Obstruction
text:
# Aortic Stenosis Valvular Obstruction

**Symptoms** Aortic stenosis causes exertional dyspnea, angina, and syncope; a harsh systolic ejection murmur radiating to the carotids and a diminished carotid upstroke are classic exam findings. Advanced disease leads to heart failure symptoms, left ventricular hypertrophy, and reduced exercise tolerance. Symptoms often progress insidiously over years. **Treatment** Medical therapy treats symptoms and comorbidities but does not reverse valve obstruction. Severe symptomatic aortic stenosis requires valve replacement—surgical aortic valve replacement (SAVR) or transcatheter aortic valve replacement (TAVR)—selected based on surgical risk, anatomy, and patient preference. Perioperative risk assessment, optimization of heart failure, and long-term follow-up are essential.

title: Arrhythmia Including Atrial Fibrillation
text:
# Arrhythmia Including Atrial Fibrillation

**Symptoms** Arrhythmias produce palpitations, lightheadedness, syncope, chest discomfort, dyspnea, or may be asymptomatic and detected incidentally. Atrial fibrillation causes irregularly irregular pulse and increases stroke risk; ventricular tachycardia or fibrillation can cause hemodynamic collapse. Underlying symptoms depend on rate, rhythm, and cardiac function. **Treatment** Management is arrhythmia-specific: for atrial fibrillation, acute rate control (beta-blockers, nondihydropyridine calcium channel blockers) or rhythm control (electrical cardioversion, antiarrhythmic drugs) is chosen based on presentation; anticoagulation is indicated according to stroke risk (CHA₂DS₂-VASc). Catheter ablation is an option for symptomatic, drug-refractory cases. Life-threatening ventricular arrhythmias require

immediate defibrillation and advanced cardiac life support; implantable cardioverter-defibrillators (ICDs) prevent sudden death in high-risk patients.

**Arthritis Osteoarthritis and Rheumatoid Arthritis**

**Symptoms** Osteoarthritis presents with joint pain worsened by use, morning stiffness that improves with activity, crepitus, and limited range of motion—commonly affecting knees, hips, hands, and spine. Rheumatoid arthritis is an inflammatory symmetric polyarthritis with prolonged morning stiffness, joint swelling, systemic fatigue, and potential extra-articular manifestations (lung, eye, vasculitis). Both cause progressive functional impairment if untreated. **Treatment** Osteoarthritis management emphasizes weight loss, exercise, physical therapy, analgesics (acetaminophen, NSAIDs), topical agents, intraarticular corticosteroids or hyaluronic acid for flares, and joint replacement for end-stage disease. Rheumatoid arthritis requires early initiation of disease-modifying antirheumatic drugs (DMARDs) such as methotrexate, with escalation to biologic agents (TNF inhibitors, IL-6 inhibitors, B-cell agents) for inadequate response; short courses of corticosteroids and NSAIDs control symptoms while DMARDs take effect. Rehabilitation and monitoring for comorbidities are important.

**Asthma Chronic Reactive Airways Disease**

**Symptoms** Asthma is characterized by episodic wheeze, cough (often nocturnal), chest tightness, and shortness of breath with variable airflow obstruction and bronchial hyperresponsiveness. Triggers include allergens, viral infections, exercise, cold air, and occupational exposures. Severity ranges from intermittent mild symptoms to life-threatening exacerbations with respiratory failure. **Treatment** Acute exacerbations are treated with inhaled short-acting beta-agonists, systemic corticosteroids, oxygen, and monitoring for respiratory compromise. Long-term control uses inhaled corticosteroids as first-line controller therapy, with addition of long-acting beta-agonists, leukotriene receptor antagonists, or biologic agents (anti-IgE, anti-IL-5/IL-4R) for severe phenotypes. Patient education, inhaler technique, trigger avoidance, and an individualized asthma action plan reduce morbidity.

**Atopic Dermatitis Eczema**

**Symptoms** Atopic dermatitis presents with chronic, intensely pruritic, relapsing eczematous lesions—erythematous, scaly, and often lichenified—commonly affecting face and extensor surfaces in infants and flexural areas in older children and adults. Scratching leads to excoriation, secondary infection, and sleep disturbance; severe disease impairs quality of life. **Treatment** Emollient therapy and skin barrier repair are foundational. Topical corticosteroids treat flares; topical calcineurin inhibitors are steroid-sparing options for sensitive areas. For moderate-to-severe disease, systemic immunomodulators (cyclosporine, methotrexate) or biologic therapy (dupilumab) may

be indicated. Identify and manage triggers, treat secondary infections, and provide patient education on long-term skin care.

title: Atherosclerosis and Peripheral Arterial Disease PAD
text:
# Atherosclerosis and Peripheral Arterial Disease PAD

**Symptoms** Atherosclerosis is the pathologic process underlying coronary, cerebral, and peripheral arterial disease and may be clinically silent until ischemic events occur. PAD typically presents with exertional claudication—reproducible calf pain with walking relieved by rest—diminished distal pulses, cool extremities, and in advanced disease nonhealing ulcers or gangrene. **Treatment** Aggressive risk-factor modification (smoking cessation, statin therapy, blood-pressure and diabetes control) is essential. Supervised exercise programs improve walking distance; antiplatelet therapy reduces cardiovascular events. Pharmacologic agents such as cilostazol may relieve claudication. Revascularization (endovascular angioplasty/stenting or surgical bypass) is reserved for lifestyle-limiting symptoms or critical limb ischemia.

title: Autism Spectrum Disorder Neurodevelopmental Condition
text:
# Autism Spectrum Disorder Neurodevelopmental Condition

**Symptoms** Autism spectrum disorder is defined by persistent deficits in social communication and interaction and restricted, repetitive patterns of behavior, interests, or activities. Symptoms appear in early childhood and vary widely in severity, often accompanied by language delay, intellectual disability, sensory sensitivities, and comorbid ADHD or anxiety. Functional impairment across social, educational, and occupational domains is common. **Treatment** Early, intensive behavioral interventions (applied behavior analysis, speech and occupational therapy) improve outcomes. Individualized educational programs, social skills training, and family support are central. Pharmacotherapy targets associated symptoms (irritability, hyperactivity, anxiety) rather than core social deficits. Lifelong supports and vocational planning help maximize independence.

title: Avascular Necrosis Osteonecrosis
text:
# Avascular Necrosis Osteonecrosis

**Symptoms** Avascular necrosis causes insidious joint pain (hip most commonly) that worsens with weight bearing and progresses to limited range of motion and joint collapse if untreated. Early disease may have minimal radiographic changes; MRI is sensitive for early detection. Risk factors include corticosteroid use, alcohol excess, trauma, and thrombophilic disorders. **Treatment** Management aims to preserve the joint and prevent collapse. Early measures include reduced weight bearing, bisphosphonates in select cases, and core decompression to relieve intraosseous pressure. Advanced disease with subchondral collapse often requires joint replacement (total hip arthroplasty). Address modifiable risk factors and consider referral to orthopedic specialists early.

Alopecia Hair Loss Disorders

**Symptoms** Alopecia presents as patterned hair thinning (androgenetic alopecia), patchy non-scarring hair loss (alopecia areata), or diffuse shedding (telogen effluvium). Onset, distribution, presence of scalp inflammation or scarring, and associated systemic symptoms guide diagnosis. Psychological distress and reduced quality of life are common. **Treatment** Androgenetic alopecia: topical minoxidil and oral finasteride (men) slow progression and promote regrowth; hair transplantation is an option for stable cases. Alopecia areata: intralesional corticosteroids for limited disease, topical immunotherapy or systemic immunomodulators for extensive disease. Telogen effluvium management focuses on identifying and treating triggers (illness, medications, nutritional deficiencies) and reassurance as hair regrowth often occurs.

title: Acid Reflux Disease GERD and Peptic Ulcer Disease
text:
# Acid Reflux Disease GERD and Peptic Ulcer Disease

**Symptoms** GERD causes heartburn, regurgitation, chest discomfort, and extra-esophageal symptoms such as chronic cough, hoarseness, or laryngitis. Peptic ulcer disease presents with epigastric pain, dyspepsia, and potential complications of bleeding or perforation. Alarm features include weight loss, anemia, dysphagia, or GI bleeding. **Treatment** Lifestyle modifications (weight loss, head-of-bed elevation, avoid late meals and trigger foods) and proton pump inhibitors (PPIs) are first-line for GERD. H. pylori testing and eradication therapy are essential for peptic ulcer disease caused by the organism; stop NSAIDs when possible and use PPI therapy for ulcer healing. Surgical or endoscopic interventions are reserved for refractory disease or complications.

title: Acute Respiratory Distress Syndrome ARDS
text:
# Acute Respiratory Distress Syndrome ARDS

**Symptoms** ARDS is an acute, diffuse inflammatory lung injury causing severe hypoxemia, bilateral pulmonary infiltrates, and respiratory failure not fully explained by cardiac failure. Common precipitants include sepsis, aspiration, severe pneumonia, trauma, and transfusion-related lung injury. Patients develop progressive dyspnea, tachypnea, and refractory hypoxemia despite supplemental oxygen. **Treatment** Management is supportive in the ICU with lung-protective mechanical ventilation (low tidal volumes, appropriate PEEP), conservative fluid strategy, treatment of the underlying cause (antibiotics for sepsis), prone positioning for severe hypoxemia, and consideration of extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (ECMO) in refractory cases. Prevent and treat complications such as ventilator-associated pneumonia and barotrauma; early rehabilitation is important for recovery.

title: Bell's Palsy Idiopathic Facial Nerve Palsy
text:
# Bell's Palsy Idiopathic Facial Nerve Palsy

**Symptoms** Bell's palsy presents with acute unilateral facial weakness affecting both the upper and lower face, often with sudden onset over hours to days. Patients may have decreased lacrimation, hyperacusis, altered taste on the anterior tongue, and difficulty closing the eye, which risks corneal exposure. Most cases are idiopathic but

may follow viral illness. **Treatment** Early short-course oral corticosteroids improve the likelihood of full recovery; antivirals may be considered in severe cases though benefit is uncertain. Protect the cornea with lubricating drops, ointment, and eye patching as needed. Physical therapy and facial retraining may aid recovery; most patients recover partially or fully within weeks to months, though some have residual weakness.

title: Appendicitis Acute Appendiceal Inflammation
text:
# Appendicitis Acute Appendiceal Inflammation

**Symptoms** Appendicitis typically begins with periumbilical pain that migrates to the right lower quadrant (McBurney point), accompanied by anorexia, nausea, vomiting, and low-grade fever. Physical exam may show localized tenderness, guarding, rebound, and positive signs such as Rovsing or psoas sign. Atypical presentations occur in children, elderly, and pregnant patients. **Treatment** Standard treatment is appendectomy (laparoscopic or open) for uncomplicated appendicitis; selected patients with early, uncomplicated disease may be managed nonoperatively with antibiotics and close follow-up. Perforated appendicitis with abscess often requires drainage and delayed appendectomy. Prompt diagnosis with clinical assessment and imaging (ultrasound or CT) reduces complications.

**Bell's Palsy (Idiopathic Facial Nerve Palsy) Symptoms** Bell's palsy presents with sudden onset unilateral facial weakness that affects both the upper and lower face, typically developing over hours to a day. Patients report inability to close the eye, drooping of the mouth, difficulty smiling, and impaired forehead movement on the affected side. Associated features can include decreased lacrimation, hyperacusis (sensitivity to sound), altered taste on the anterior two-thirds of the tongue, and mild pain or discomfort around the ear preceding weakness. On exam there is flaccid paralysis of facial muscles with preserved sensation; absence of forehead sparing helps distinguish peripheral facial nerve palsy from central lesions. Most cases are idiopathic but may follow viral prodromes (herpes simplex or zoster) or occur with diabetes or pregnancy. **Treatment** Early treatment with a short course of oral corticosteroids (prednisone) started within 72 hours of onset improves the likelihood of full recovery. Antiviral therapy (acyclovir or valacyclovir) may be added when herpes zoster or severe palsy is suspected, though benefit is modest. Eye care is essential: lubricating drops, ointment at night, and protective patching to prevent corneal drying and injury when eyelid closure is incomplete. Physical therapy and facial retraining exercises can aid functional recovery. Most patients recover substantially within weeks to months; referral to neurology or ENT is indicated for atypical features, progressive weakness, or lack of improvement.

**Benign Prostatic Hyperplasia (BPH) Symptoms** BPH is a nonmalignant enlargement of the prostate common in older men that produces lower urinary tract symptoms (LUTS). Typical complaints include urinary frequency, nocturia, urgency, weak urinary stream, hesitancy, straining, incomplete bladder emptying, and post-void dribbling.

Severe obstruction can lead to urinary retention, recurrent urinary tract infections, bladder stones, or renal impairment. Symptom severity is often graded using validated questionnaires (e.g., IPSS). **Treatment** Management is tailored to symptom severity and patient preference. Watchful waiting with lifestyle measures (fluid timing, reducing caffeine/alcohol) is appropriate for mild symptoms. Medical therapy includes alpha-1 blockers (tamsulosin, terazosin) for rapid symptom relief and 5-alpha-reductase inhibitors (finasteride, dutasteride) to reduce prostate volume over months and lower long-term risk of progression. Combination therapy is used for moderate-to-severe symptoms. Minimally invasive procedures (transurethral microwave therapy, UroLift) and surgical options (transurethral resection of the prostate, open prostatectomy) are reserved for refractory symptoms, complications, or very large prostates. Evaluate for prostate cancer when indicated by PSA, exam, or atypical features.

**Birth Defects (Congenital Anomalies) Symptoms** Birth defects encompass structural or functional anomalies present at birth that range from minor cosmetic differences to life-threatening malformations. Examples include neural tube defects (spina bifida), congenital heart defects (ventricular septal defect, tetralogy of Fallot), limb anomalies, cleft lip/palate, and chromosomal syndromes (Down syndrome). Clinical presentation varies by defect: cyanosis or heart murmur in cardiac lesions, neurologic deficits in neural tube defects, feeding difficulties with cleft palate, and growth or developmental delays with genetic syndromes. Many anomalies are detected prenatally by ultrasound or newborn screening. **Treatment** Management depends on the specific anomaly and severity. Some defects require immediate neonatal stabilization and surgical correction (complex congenital heart disease, intestinal atresia), while others benefit from staged surgical repair (cleft lip/palate) and multidisciplinary rehabilitation (physical therapy, speech therapy). Genetic counseling, early intervention services, and long-term follow-up for developmental, educational, and medical needs are essential. Prevention strategies include periconceptional folic acid to reduce neural tube defects, avoidance of teratogens, and management of maternal conditions (diabetes, infections).

**Bleeding Disorders and Hemophilia Symptoms** Bleeding disorders include inherited conditions (hemophilia A/B, von Willebrand disease) and acquired coagulopathies. Hemophilia typically presents with prolonged bleeding after trauma or surgery, spontaneous joint and muscle hemorrhages, and easy bruising; severity correlates with factor deficiency level. Von Willebrand disease causes mucocutaneous bleeding—epistaxis, menorrhagia, easy bruising—and may be mild and intermittent. Acquired disorders (liver disease, vitamin K deficiency, anticoagulant therapy) produce variable bleeding risk including GI bleeding and intracranial hemorrhage. **Treatment** Treatment is diagnosis-specific. Hemophilia A/B is treated with replacement of deficient clotting factor concentrates (factor VIII or IX), prophylactic regimens to prevent joint damage in severe disease, and desmopressin (DDAVP) for mild hemophilia A. Von Willebrand disease management includes DDAVP for responsive types, von Willebrand factor

concentrates for severe cases, and antifibrinolytic agents (tranexamic acid) for mucosal bleeding. Acquired coagulopathies require correction of underlying causes, vitamin K, plasma or prothrombin complex concentrates for urgent reversal, and careful management of anticoagulant therapy.

# Sickle Cell Disease and Thalassemia (Inherited Hemoglobinopathies) Symptoms

Sickle cell disease causes episodic vaso-occlusive pain crises, chronic hemolytic anemia, fatigue, jaundice, splenic dysfunction with infection risk, acute chest syndrome, stroke, and end-organ damage. Thalassemias range from asymptomatic trait to transfusion-dependent major forms; severe disease presents with profound anemia, growth retardation, bone deformities from marrow expansion, and iron overload from transfusions. Both disorders often manifest in childhood. **Treatment** Sickle cell management includes pain control, hydration, oxygen, infection prevention (vaccination, penicillin prophylaxis in young children), hydroxyurea to reduce vaso-occlusive events, chronic transfusion for stroke prevention, and curative hematopoietic stem cell transplantation in selected patients. Thalassemia major requires regular transfusions with iron chelation therapy to prevent iron overload; splenectomy and bone marrow transplantation are options in selected cases. Newer gene-based therapies are emerging for both conditions.

# Bone Marrow Transplantation (Hematopoietic Stem Cell Transplant) Symptoms

Indications for bone marrow transplantation include hematologic malignancies (leukemia, lymphoma), severe aplastic anemia, certain inherited metabolic or immune disorders, and some hemoglobinopathies. Patients considered for transplant may present with cytopenias, recurrent infections, bleeding, or disease-specific symptoms. Pretransplant evaluation assesses disease status, organ function, donor availability, and psychosocial readiness. **Treatment** Hematopoietic stem cell transplantation involves conditioning chemotherapy ± radiation to eradicate disease and immunosuppress the host, followed by infusion of donor or autologous stem cells. Posttransplant care focuses on infection prophylaxis, graft-versus-host disease prevention and management, monitoring for engraftment and complications (veno-occlusive disease, organ toxicity), and long-term surveillance for relapse and late effects. Outcomes depend on disease, donor match, patient age, and comorbidities.

occurs. Administration of antitoxin (equine-derived or human botulism immune globulin for infant botulism) neutralizes circulating toxin but does not reverse established paralysis. Wound debridement and antibiotics are indicated for wound botulism (avoid aminoglycosides). Recovery may take weeks to months with intensive rehabilitation.

**Bronchiectasis Symptoms** Bronchiectasis is characterized by chronic productive cough with large volumes of purulent sputum, recurrent respiratory infections, hemoptysis, dyspnea, and fatigue. Physical exam may reveal crackles and wheeze; clubbing occurs in some patients. Causes include prior severe infections, cystic fibrosis, immune deficiency, or airway obstruction. CT chest demonstrates bronchial dilation and wall thickening. **Treatment** Management aims to control infection, reduce sputum burden, and prevent exacerbations. Airway clearance techniques (physiotherapy, postural drainage), regular exercise, and mucolytics help sputum clearance. Antibiotics treat acute exacerbations and may be used long-term in selected patients with frequent infections; inhaled antibiotics are an option for chronic Pseudomonas infection. Vaccination, bronchodilators for coexisting airway disease, and surgical resection for localized disease refractory to medical therapy are additional strategies.

**Bronchiolitis (Infants and Young Children) Symptoms** Bronchiolitis is an acute viral lower respiratory tract infection most commonly caused by respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) in infants and young children. It presents with rhinorrhea, cough, tachypnea, wheeze, crackles, feeding difficulty, and varying degrees of respiratory distress. High-risk infants (premature, chronic lung disease, congenital heart disease) are more likely to require hospitalization. **Treatment** Care is primarily supportive: hydration, nasal suctioning, oxygen for hypoxemia, and monitoring for respiratory failure. Bronchodilators and corticosteroids are not routinely recommended but may be trialed in selected patients with reactive airways. Severe cases require hospitalization for respiratory support, including high-flow nasal cannula or mechanical ventilation. Prevention includes hand hygiene and RSV prophylaxis (palivizumab) for high-risk infants.

**Bacterial Meningitis (Acute Meningitis) Symptoms** Acute bacterial meningitis presents with fever, severe headache, neck stiffness (nuchal rigidity), photophobia, altered mental status, and sometimes focal neurologic deficits or seizures. Infants may show nonspecific signs—poor feeding, irritability, bulging fontanelle. Rapid progression and high morbidity/mortality make early recognition critical. Common pathogens vary by age (Group B Streptococcus and E. coli in neonates; Streptococcus pneumoniae and Neisseria meningitidis in older children and adults). **Treatment** Immediate empiric intravenous antibiotics that penetrate the CSF are essential after obtaining blood cultures and, when safe, lumbar puncture. Empiric regimens are age- and risk-based and often include a third-generation cephalosporin plus vancomycin; ampicillin is

added for Listeria coverage in older adults and neonates. Adjunctive dexamethasone reduces neurologic complications in pneumococcal meningitis when given before or with the first antibiotic dose. Supportive care, close monitoring for complications (seizures, increased intracranial pressure), and public health measures (prophylaxis for close contacts in meningococcal disease) are required.

**Bacterial Endocarditis (Infective Endocarditis) Symptoms** Infective endocarditis presents with fever, new or changing heart murmur, fatigue, anorexia, weight loss, and signs of embolic phenomena (splinter hemorrhages, Janeway lesions, stroke, splenic infarcts). Subacute presentations may be indolent, while acute staphylococcal infections can be fulminant. Risk factors include prosthetic valves, prior endocarditis, intravenous drug use, and structural heart disease. Blood cultures and echocardiography (transesophageal preferred) are key to diagnosis. **Treatment** Management requires prolonged, targeted intravenous antibiotics based on culture and sensitivity, often for 4–6 weeks. Early involvement of infectious disease and cardiothoracic surgery teams is important; surgical valve repair or replacement is indicated for heart failure, uncontrolled infection, large vegetations with embolic risk, or prosthetic valve involvement. Supportive care and prevention (dental hygiene, appropriate prophylaxis in high-risk procedures) are part of comprehensive management.

**Bladder Cancer Symptoms** Bladder cancer most commonly presents with painless gross hematuria. Other symptoms include urinary frequency, urgency, dysuria, and pelvic pain in advanced disease. Risk factors include tobacco smoking, occupational exposures (aromatic amines), chronic bladder inflammation, and prior pelvic radiation. Most tumors are urothelial (transitional cell) carcinomas. **Treatment** Evaluation includes cystoscopy with biopsy and imaging to stage disease. Non-muscle-invasive tumors are treated with transurethral resection and intravesical therapy (BCG or chemotherapy) to reduce recurrence. Muscle-invasive disease often requires radical cystectomy with urinary diversion, systemic chemotherapy for locally advanced or metastatic disease, and bladder-sparing multimodality therapy in selected patients. Surveillance for recurrence is intensive due to high recurrence rates.

**Brain Tumors (Primary and Metastatic) Symptoms** Symptoms depend on tumor location, size, and growth rate and may include persistent headache (often worse in the morning), seizures, focal neurologic deficits (weakness, sensory loss, aphasia, visual field deficits), cognitive or personality changes, nausea, and signs of increased intracranial pressure. Primary brain tumors (gliomas, meningiomas) and metastatic lesions from lung, breast, melanoma, kidney, or colon are common. Imaging with MRI is the diagnostic modality of choice. **Treatment** Management is multidisciplinary and may include surgical resection for diagnosis and cytoreduction, radiation therapy (conformal, stereotactic radiosurgery), and systemic therapies (chemotherapy, targeted

agents, immunotherapy) depending on tumor histology and molecular markers. Supportive care addresses seizures (antiepileptics), corticosteroids for vasogenic edema, rehabilitation, and palliative measures. Prognosis varies widely by tumor type, grade, and patient factors.

Cancer (General) Symptoms Cancer symptoms vary by organ and tumor type but commonly include unexplained weight loss, persistent fatigue, localized pain or mass, changes in bowel or bladder habits, persistent cough or hoarseness, unexplained bleeding, and systemic signs such as fever or night sweats. Early disease may be asymptomatic; screening tests (mammography, colonoscopy, Pap test) detect many cancers before symptoms appear. Treatment Treatment is tumor-specific and may combine surgery, radiation therapy, systemic chemotherapy, targeted biologic agents, immunotherapy, and supportive/palliative care. Staging guides therapy; multidisciplinary teams tailor curative or palliative approaches, manage treatment toxicities, and provide survivorship planning.
Cataracts Symptoms Progressive, painless blurring of vision, glare (especially at night), halos around lights, faded colors, and difficulty reading or driving. Symptoms worsen gradually as the lens becomes opacified. Treatment Early cataracts may be managed with refractive correction and brighter lighting; definitive treatment is surgical removal of the cloudy lens with intraocular lens implantation (phacoemulsification), which restores vision in the majority of patients. Perioperative care includes topical antibiotics and anti-inflammatory agents.
Cellulitis Symptoms Acute, spreading erythema, warmth, swelling, and tenderness of skin and subcutaneous tissues; fever and regional lymphadenopathy may accompany more severe infection. Commonly follows a break in the skin. Treatment Empiric oral or IV antibiotics targeting streptococci and staphylococci (choice guided by severity and MRSA prevalence), elevation and immobilization of the limb, analgesia, and drainage if an abscess is present. Hospitalization for systemic signs or immunocompromise.
Cerebral Aneurysm (Subarachnoid Hemorrhage) Symptoms Unruptured aneurysms are often asymptomatic; rupture causes sudden, severe "thunderclap" headache, neck stiffness, photophobia, nausea, vomiting, loss of consciousness, and focal neurologic deficits. Early recognition is critical. Treatment Emergency stabilization, neuroimaging (CT, angiography), neurosurgical or endovascular repair (clipping or coiling) to secure the aneurysm, and intensive care management to control intracranial pressure, vasospasm, and complications. Long-term follow-up and risk-factor control are essential.
Cerebral Palsy Symptoms Nonprogressive motor impairment from early brain injury presenting with spasticity, dyskinesia, or ataxia; delayed motor milestones, abnormal

tone, and gait disturbances; associated impairments may include intellectual disability, seizures, vision or hearing problems, and speech difficulties. **Treatment** Multidisciplinary rehabilitation (physical, occupational, speech therapy), spasticity management (oral medications, botulinum toxin, intrathecal baclofen), orthopedic interventions for contractures, seizure control, and educational supports to maximize function and participation.

🧾 **Cervical Cancer Symptoms** Early cervical cancer is often asymptomatic; later signs include abnormal vaginal bleeding (postcoital or intermenstrual), pelvic pain, and abnormal Pap test results. Screening with Pap smears and HPV testing reduces incidence and mortality. **Treatment** Management depends on stage: local excision (LEEP, conization) for preinvasive disease; radical surgery (hysterectomy) and/or radiation with concurrent chemotherapy for invasive disease; fertility-sparing options considered in selected early cases. Follow-up includes surveillance for recurrence.

🧾 **Chickenpox (Varicella) and Shingles (Herpes Zoster) Symptoms** Varicella: fever and a pruritic vesicular rash in successive crops; complications include bacterial superinfection and pneumonia in adults. Herpes zoster: painful, unilateral dermatomal vesicular eruption with risk of postherpetic neuralgia. **Treatment** Varicella is usually supportive (antihistamines, skin care); antivirals (acyclovir) for adults or immunocompromised patients. Herpes zoster: early antiviral therapy reduces severity and duration; analgesics, topical care, and neuropathic pain agents (gabapentin, TCAs) for postherpetic neuralgia. Vaccination prevents or reduces severity.

🧾 **Chronic Kidney Disease (Chronic Kidney Failure) Symptoms** Gradual fatigue, anorexia, nausea, pruritus, edema, anemia, electrolyte disturbances, and uremic symptoms as glomerular filtration declines; hypertension and bone-mineral disorders are common. **Treatment** Slow progression with blood-pressure control (ACE inhibitors/ARBs), glycemic control in diabetes, dietary measures, anemia management (erythropoiesis-stimulating agents, iron), and timely referral for renal replacement therapy (dialysis or transplantation) when indicated. Address reversible causes and provide cardiovascular risk reduction.

🧾 **Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease (COPD) / Chronic Bronchitis / Emphysema Symptoms** Chronic productive cough, progressive dyspnea, wheeze, and exercise intolerance; exacerbations with increased sputum purulence and breathlessness; advanced disease leads to hypoxemia and hypercapnia. **Treatment** Smoking cessation is paramount. Pharmacotherapy includes bronchodilators (short- and long-acting beta-agonists, anticholinergics), inhaled corticosteroids for frequent exacerbations, pulmonary rehabilitation, oxygen therapy for chronic hypoxemia, and vaccinations. Manage exacerbations with bronchodilators, systemic steroids, and antibiotics when indicated.

Manage complications: diuretics and paracentesis for ascites, endoscopic therapy and beta-blockers for varices, lactulose for encephalopathy, and liver transplantation for decompensated cirrhosis. Preventive measures include vaccination and alcohol counseling.

☐ **Colon Cancer (Colorectal Cancer) Symptoms** Painless rectal bleeding, change in bowel habits, unexplained iron-deficiency anemia, abdominal pain, and weight loss; many early cancers are detected by screening colonoscopy or fecal occult blood testing. **Treatment** Surgical resection is the mainstay for localized disease; adjuvant chemotherapy for stage II/III disease and systemic therapy for metastatic disease (chemotherapy, targeted agents, immunotherapy depending on molecular profile). Screening and polypectomy prevent many cancers.

☐ **Concussion and Traumatic Brain Injury (TBI) Symptoms** Transient confusion, headache, dizziness, nausea, memory impairment, sleep disturbance, and sometimes loss of consciousness after head trauma; persistent post-concussive symptoms can last weeks to months. Severe TBI causes focal deficits, prolonged unconsciousness, and cognitive/behavioral changes. **Treatment** Initial assessment for red flags and imaging when indicated; cognitive and physical rest followed by graded return to activity for concussion. Severe TBI requires neurosurgical and intensive care management, rehabilitation (physical, occupational, speech therapy), and long-term neuropsychological support.

☐ **Congenital Heart Disease Symptoms** Presentations range from cyanosis and heart failure in neonates to exertional dyspnea, murmurs, and exercise intolerance in older children and adults; specific defects (VSD, ASD, tetralogy of Fallot, transposition) have characteristic clinical patterns. **Treatment** Management includes medical therapy for heart failure and arrhythmias, catheter-based interventions (device closure, balloon valvuloplasty), and surgical repair or palliation depending on defect type and severity. Lifelong cardiology follow-up is often required.

☐ **Coronary Artery Disease (Ischemic Heart Disease) Symptoms** Stable angina (exertional chest discomfort), acute coronary syndromes (unstable angina, myocardial infarction) with chest pain, diaphoresis, dyspnea, nausea, and sometimes atypical presentations in women and elderly. Chronic ischemia causes heart failure and arrhythmias. **Treatment** Acute MI requires rapid reperfusion (PCI or thrombolysis), antiplatelet therapy, anticoagulation, and supportive care. Long-term management includes antiplatelet agents, statins, beta-blockers, ACE inhibitors, lifestyle

modification, cardiac rehabilitation, and revascularization when indicated. Risk-factor control is central to prevention.

- Crohn's Disease (Inflammatory Bowel Disease) Symptoms Chronic abdominal pain, diarrhea (often bloody), weight loss, fever, and perianal disease; transmural inflammation can cause strictures, fistulae, and malabsorption. Extraintestinal manifestations include arthritis, skin lesions, and eye inflammation. Treatment Induction with corticosteroids for flares; maintenance with immunomodulators (azathioprine, methotrexate) or biologic agents (anti-TNF, anti-integrin, anti-IL-12/23) to control inflammation and prevent complications. Nutritional support, antibiotics for abscesses, and surgery for strictures or refractory disease are part of care.
- Cystic Fibrosis Symptoms Chronic productive cough, recurrent pulmonary infections, bronchiectasis, malabsorption with steatorrhea and failure to thrive, male infertility, and salt-loss in infancy. Progressive lung disease is the major cause of morbidity and mortality. Treatment Multidisciplinary care: airway clearance techniques, inhaled bronchodilators and mucolytics, chronic suppressive antibiotics for Pseudomonas, pancreatic enzyme replacement, nutritional support, CFTR-modulator therapies for eligible mutations, and lung transplantation for end-stage disease. Vaccination and infection control are important.
- Deep Vein Thrombosis (DVT) and Pulmonary Embolism (PE) Symptoms DVT: unilateral leg swelling, pain, warmth, and erythema. PE: sudden dyspnea, pleuritic chest pain, tachycardia, hypoxemia, and sometimes syncope. Both can be life-threatening. Treatment Anticoagulation (heparin followed by oral anticoagulants or direct oral anticoagulants) is the mainstay; thrombolysis for massive PE with hemodynamic compromise; IVC filters for contraindications to anticoagulation; compression stockings and risk-factor modification for prevention. Evaluate for provoking factors and consider extended therapy when indicated.
- Dementia (including Alzheimer Disease) Symptoms Progressive decline in memory, executive function, language, and visuospatial skills with behavioral changes; Alzheimer disease is the most common cause, but vascular, Lewy body, and frontotemporal dementias have distinct features. Functional impairment in daily activities is typical. Treatment Cholinesterase inhibitors and memantine provide modest symptomatic benefit in Alzheimer disease; address reversible causes, manage behavioral symptoms with nonpharmacologic strategies first, and provide caregiver support, safety planning, and long-term care coordination.
- Depressive Disorders (Major Depression) Symptoms Persistent low mood, anhedonia, sleep and appetite changes, fatigue, impaired concentration, feelings of worthlessness or guilt, and suicidal ideation. Severity ranges from mild to severe with psychotic features. Treatment Evidence-based care includes psychotherapy (CBT,

interpersonal therapy), antidepressant medications (SSRIs, SNRIs, others), and for severe or treatment-resistant cases, electroconvulsive therapy or newer neuromodulation techniques. Safety assessment and management of comorbidities are essential.

- Diabetes Mellitus (Type 1 and Type 2) Symptoms Polyuria, polydipsia, polyphagia, weight loss (type 1), fatigue, blurred vision, and complications such as neuropathy, nephropathy, retinopathy, and cardiovascular disease with chronic hyperglycemia. Treatment Type 1 requires lifelong insulin therapy, glucose monitoring, and education. Type 2 management includes lifestyle modification, oral agents (metformin first-line), GLP-1 receptor agonists or SGLT2 inhibitors for cardiovascular/renal benefit, and insulin when needed. Preventive care for complications and individualized glycemic targets are important.
- Diverticulitis (Diverticulosis and Complications) Symptoms Diverticulosis is often asymptomatic; diverticulitis presents with left lower-quadrant abdominal pain, fever, leukocytosis, and possible complications—abscess, perforation, fistula, or obstruction. Treatment Uncomplicated diverticulitis: bowel rest, antibiotics, and outpatient management for mild cases. Complicated disease may require percutaneous drainage of abscesses or surgical resection for perforation, recurrent episodes, or fistula. Long-term prevention includes high-fiber diet and risk-factor modification.
- Epilepsy and Seizure Disorders Symptoms Recurrent unprovoked seizures with variable manifestations—focal motor or sensory events, impaired awareness, generalized tonic-clonic convulsions. Postictal confusion and injury risk are common. Etiologies include structural brain lesions, genetic syndromes, metabolic disturbances, and idiopathic causes. Treatment Antiepileptic drugs chosen by seizure type (carbamazepine, valproate, levetiracetam, etc.), lifestyle counseling, seizure precautions, and for refractory focal epilepsy, surgical resection, vagus nerve stimulation, or ketogenic diet in selected patients. Address reversible triggers and comorbidities.
- Fibromyalgia Symptoms Chronic widespread musculoskeletal pain, fatigue, sleep disturbance, cognitive complaints ("fibro fog"), and multiple tender points; symptoms often follow physical or emotional stressors. Treatment Multimodal approach: patient education, graded exercise, cognitive behavioral therapy, sleep hygiene, and pharmacotherapy (duloxetine, pregabalin, low-dose amitriptyline) for symptom control. Address comorbid mood disorders and encourage self-management strategies.
- Gallstones (Cholelithiasis) and Cholecystitis Symptoms Biliary colic—episodic right upper-quadrant or epigastric pain often after fatty meals; acute cholecystitis causes persistent severe RUQ pain, fever, leukocytosis, and Murphy sign. Complications include choledocholithiasis and pancreatitis. Treatment Symptomatic

gallstones: elective laparoscopic cholecystectomy. Acute cholecystitis: initial resuscitation, antibiotics, and early cholecystectomy or percutaneous cholecystostomy in high-risk patients. ERCP for common bile duct stones when present.

**Headache (Primary and Secondary Headaches) Symptoms** Headache presents as pain in the head or upper neck and ranges from episodic tension-type headaches (bilateral, pressing/tightening) to migraine (unilateral, pulsatile, moderate-to-severe, often with photophobia, phonophobia, nausea, and aura) and cluster headaches (severe unilateral periorbital pain with autonomic features). Secondary headaches arise from underlying causes—sinusitis, meningitis, intracranial hemorrhage, tumor, temporal arteritis, or medication overuse—and may have red flags: sudden onset “thunderclap” pain, focal neurologic signs, fever, progressive worsening, or new headache in older adults. **Treatment** Primary headaches: acute migraine therapy includes NSAIDs, triptans, antiemetics, and rest in a dark, quiet environment; preventive therapy (beta-blockers, antiepileptics, antidepressants, CGRP inhibitors) is used for frequent or disabling attacks. Tension-type headaches respond to analgesics, stress management, and physical therapy. Cluster headaches may require high-flow oxygen, subcutaneous sumatriptan, and preventive agents (verapamil). Secondary headaches require treatment of the underlying cause (antibiotics for meningitis, urgent neurosurgical care for hemorrhage, corticosteroids for temporal arteritis). Avoid medication overuse and address triggers.

Right-sided failure produces hepatomegaly and ascites; left-sided failure leads to pulmonary congestion. Acute decompensation presents with severe dyspnea, hypoxia, and hypotension. **Treatment** Management includes diuretics for volume overload, ACE inhibitors or ARBs (or ARNI), beta-blockers, mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists, and SGLT2 inhibitors to improve symptoms and survival. Device therapy (ICD, CRT) and advanced options (inotropes, mechanical circulatory support, transplantation) are used for selected patients. Treat precipitating causes (ischemia, arrhythmia, infection), optimize comorbidities, and provide patient education on sodium/fluid restriction and self-monitoring.

Acute viral hepatitis (A, B, C, D, E) may be symptomatic or subclinical; chronic hepatitis (B, C) leads to progressive fibrosis, cirrhosis, and hepatocellular carcinoma risk. Alcoholic and nonalcoholic steatohepatitis cause similar features with metabolic risk factors. **Treatment** Acute supportive care for symptomatic viral hepatitis A/E; antiviral therapy for chronic

Secondary headaches arise from underlying causes—sinusitis, meningitis, intracranial hemorrhage, tumor, temporal arteritis, or medication overuse—and may have red flags: sudden onset “thunderclap” pain, focal neurologic signs, fever, progressive worsening, or new headache in older adults. **Treatment** Primary headaches: acute migraine therapy includes NSAIDs, triptans, antiemetics, and rest in a dark, quiet environment; preventive therapy (beta-blockers, antiepileptics, antidepressants, CGRP inhibitors) is used for frequent or disabling attacks. Tension-type headaches respond to analgesics, stress management, and physical therapy. Cluster headaches may require high-flow oxygen, subcutaneous sumatriptan, and preventive agents (verapamil). Secondary headaches require treatment of the underlying cause (antibiotics for meningitis, urgent neurosurgical care for hemorrhage, corticosteroids for temporal arteritis). Avoid medication overuse and address triggers.

**Heart Failure (Congestive Heart Failure) Symptoms** Heart failure causes exertional dyspnea, orthopnea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea, fatigue, reduced exercise tolerance, peripheral edema, and signs of fluid overload (jugular venous distension, pulmonary crackles). Right-sided failure produces hepatomegaly and ascites; left-sided failure leads to pulmonary congestion. Acute decompensation presents with severe dyspnea, hypoxia, and hypotension. **Treatment** Management includes diuretics for volume overload, ACE inhibitors or ARBs (or ARNI), beta-blockers, mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists, and SGLT2 inhibitors to improve symptoms and survival. Device therapy (ICD, CRT) and advanced options (inotropes, mechanical circulatory support, transplantation) are used for selected patients. Treat precipitating causes (ischemia, arrhythmia, infection), optimize comorbidities, and provide patient education on sodium/fluid restriction and self-monitoring.

**Hepatitis (Viral and Nonviral Liver Inflammation) Symptoms** Hepatitis presents with fatigue, anorexia, nausea, right upper-quadrant discomfort, jaundice, dark urine, pale stools, and elevated liver enzymes. Acute viral hepatitis (A, B, C, D, E) may be symptomatic or subclinical; chronic hepatitis (B, C) leads to progressive fibrosis, cirrhosis, and hepatocellular carcinoma risk. Alcoholic and nonalcoholic steatohepatitis cause similar features with metabolic risk factors. **Treatment** Acute supportive care for symptomatic viral hepatitis A/E; antiviral therapy for chronic

hepatitis B (nucleos(t)ide analogues) and hepatitis C (direct-acting antivirals) to achieve viral suppression or cure. Manage complications of chronic liver disease (portal hypertension, varices, encephalopathy) and counsel on alcohol cessation, weight loss for NAFLD, vaccination (A, B), and screening for hepatocellular carcinoma in high-risk patients.

**HIV Infection (Human Immunodeficiency Virus) Symptoms** Early HIV infection may be asymptomatic or present with a mononucleosis-like illness (fever, sore throat, lymphadenopathy, rash). Progressive untreated infection leads to immunosuppression, opportunistic infections, weight loss, chronic diarrhea, and AIDS-defining illnesses. Laboratory markers include declining CD4+ T-cell counts and rising viral load.

**Treatment** Antiretroviral therapy (ART) combining agents from different classes (integrase inhibitors, NRTIs, NNRTIs, protease inhibitors) suppresses viral replication, restores immune function, and reduces transmission. Treatment is individualized based on resistance testing and comorbidities. Preventive measures include PrEP for high-risk individuals and PEP after exposure. Manage opportunistic infections, provide vaccinations when appropriate, and offer psychosocial support and adherence counseling.

**Hypertension (High Blood Pressure) Symptoms** Hypertension is often asymptomatic; when present, symptoms are nonspecific—headache, dizziness, visual changes, or palpitations. Long-standing uncontrolled hypertension causes end-organ damage: left ventricular hypertrophy, coronary artery disease, stroke, chronic kidney disease, and retinopathy. Hypertensive emergencies present with acute end-organ dysfunction (encephalopathy, myocardial ischemia, renal failure). **Treatment** Lifestyle modifications (dietary sodium reduction, DASH diet, weight loss, exercise, alcohol moderation) and pharmacotherapy (thiazide diuretics, ACE inhibitors, ARBs, calcium channel blockers, beta-blockers) tailored to comorbidities. Target blood-pressure goals individualized by age and risk. In hypertensive emergencies, controlled IV antihypertensives in an ICU setting are required. Regular monitoring and adherence support reduce cardiovascular risk.

### Hyperthyroidism and Hypothyroidism (Thyroid Disorders) Symptoms

Hyperthyroidism: weight loss, heat intolerance, palpitations, tremor, anxiety, increased appetite, and goiter; severe cases cause atrial fibrillation and thyrotoxic crisis. Hypothyroidism: fatigue, weight gain, cold intolerance, constipation, dry skin, bradycardia, and cognitive slowing; severe hypothyroidism (myxedema) can be life-threatening. **Treatment** Hyperthyroidism: antithyroid drugs (methimazole, propylthiouracil), radioactive iodine ablation, or surgery for definitive therapy; beta-blockers for symptomatic control. Hypothyroidism: lifelong levothyroxine replacement with dose titration by TSH levels. Treat precipitating causes and monitor for complications (cardiac disease, osteoporosis).

**Influenza (Seasonal Flu) Symptoms** Influenza causes abrupt onset fever, myalgia, headache, cough, sore throat, and malaise; complications include pneumonia, exacerbation of chronic cardiopulmonary disease, and secondary bacterial infections, particularly in the elderly and immunocompromised. **Treatment** Antiviral agents (oseltamivir, zanamivir, baloxavir) are most effective when started early and reduce symptom duration and complications in high-risk patients. Supportive care includes hydration, antipyretics, and rest. Annual vaccination is the primary preventive strategy and reduces severe outcomes.

**Ischemic Stroke and Transient Ischemic Attack (TIA) Symptoms** Sudden focal neurologic deficits—weakness or numbness of face/arm/leg (usually unilateral), speech disturbance, visual loss, dizziness, or ataxia. TIAs produce transient deficits that resolve within 24 hours but signal high stroke risk. Rapid recognition and time-sensitive evaluation are critical. **Treatment** Acute ischemic stroke: urgent assessment for reperfusion therapy (IV thrombolysis within time window, mechanical thrombectomy for large-vessel occlusion) and supportive care. Secondary prevention includes antiplatelet or anticoagulant therapy (for cardioembolic sources), blood-pressure and lipid control, diabetes management, smoking cessation, and carotid intervention when indicated. Rehabilitation addresses functional recovery.

**Irritable Bowel Syndrome (IBS) and Functional GI Disorders Symptoms** IBS presents with recurrent abdominal pain associated with altered bowel habits (constipation, diarrhea, or mixed), bloating, and relief with defecation. Symptoms are chronic and fluctuate, often triggered by stress or certain foods. No structural disease is found on routine testing. **Treatment** Management is symptom-directed: dietary modification (low-FODMAP diet), fiber supplementation, antispasmodics, laxatives or antidiarrheals as needed, and psychological therapies (CBT, gut-directed hypnotherapy). Address comorbid anxiety or depression and provide patient education on chronicity and self-management.

**Kidney Stones (Nephrolithiasis) Symptoms** Renal colic presents with sudden, severe flank pain radiating to the groin, hematuria, nausea, and vomiting. Fever suggests superimposed infection and requires urgent attention. Stone size and location determine symptoms and passage likelihood. **Treatment** Pain control, hydration, and medical expulsive therapy (alpha-blockers) for small distal stones. Larger stones or obstructing stones with infection require urologic intervention—ureteroscopy with laser lithotripsy, shock-wave lithotripsy, or percutaneous nephrolithotomy. Preventive measures include metabolic evaluation, dietary modification, and medications (thiazides, citrate) tailored to stone composition.

**Liver Cancer (Hepatocellular Carcinoma) Symptoms** Often asymptomatic early; later signs include weight loss, abdominal pain, hepatomegaly, jaundice, ascites, and decompensation in cirrhotic patients. Screening in high-risk populations (cirrhosis,

chronic hepatitis B/C) detects tumors earlier. **Treatment** Curative options for early disease include surgical resection, liver transplantation, or ablative therapies. Intermediate and advanced disease may be treated with transarterial chemoembolization, targeted systemic therapies (tyrosine kinase inhibitors), and immunotherapy. Management includes surveillance, treatment of underlying liver disease, and palliative care when needed.

**Lung Cancer Symptoms** Persistent cough, hemoptysis, dyspnea, chest pain, unexplained weight loss, and paraneoplastic syndromes. Many cases are detected at advanced stages; smoking is the primary risk factor. **Treatment** Management depends on histology and stage: surgical resection for early disease, radiation therapy, systemic chemotherapy, targeted therapies for driver mutations (EGFR, ALK, ROS1), and immunotherapy for advanced disease. Smoking cessation, screening in high-risk individuals, and multidisciplinary care improve outcomes.

**Lyme Disease (Borrelia burgdorferi Infection) Symptoms** Early localized disease: erythema migrans rash (expanding target lesion), fever, fatigue, headache, and myalgias. Disseminated disease causes multiple rashes, neurologic involvement (facial palsy, meningitis), and cardiac conduction abnormalities. Late disease may produce arthritis and neurologic symptoms. **Treatment** Early disease: oral doxycycline (or amoxicillin/cefuroxime in children/pregnancy) for 10–21 days. Disseminated or neurologic disease may require IV ceftriaxone. Symptom management and follow-up for persistent symptoms are individualized; prevention includes tick avoidance and prompt removal.

**Malaria Symptoms** Cyclical fevers, chills, sweats, headache, myalgias, malaise, and in severe cases anemia, jaundice, respiratory distress, cerebral involvement, and multiorgan failure. Travel history to endemic areas is key to diagnosis. **Treatment** Species-specific antimalarial therapy (artemisinin-based combination therapy for P. falciparum in many regions; chloroquine for sensitive strains). Severe malaria requires parenteral therapy (IV artesunate) and intensive supportive care. Prevention includes chemoprophylaxis for travelers, insecticide-treated bed nets, and vector control.

**Melanoma and Skin Cancer Symptoms** New or changing pigmented lesion, asymmetry, border irregularity, color variation, diameter >6 mm, or evolution (ABCDE). Nonmelanoma skin cancers (basal cell, squamous cell) present as nonhealing nodules or ulcers. Early detection improves prognosis. **Treatment** Surgical excision with appropriate margins is primary therapy; sentinel lymph node biopsy for staging in melanoma. Advanced melanoma may be treated with immunotherapy (checkpoint inhibitors) and targeted agents for BRAF-mutant tumors. Prevention includes sun protection and skin surveillance.

**Multiple Sclerosis (MS) Symptoms** Relapsing-remitting or progressive neurologic deficits—optic neuritis, limb weakness, sensory disturbances, ataxia, bladder dysfunction, and cognitive changes—reflecting demyelinating lesions in the CNS. Symptoms often fluctuate and accumulate over time. **Treatment** Acute relapses treated with high-dose corticosteroids; disease-modifying therapies (interferons, glatiramer acetate, monoclonal antibodies, oral agents) reduce relapse rate and slow progression. Symptomatic therapies, rehabilitation, and multidisciplinary care address spasticity, fatigue, bladder dysfunction, and mood disorders.

**Myocardial Infarction (Heart Attack) Symptoms** Chest pain or pressure often radiating to jaw, neck, shoulder, or arm, accompanied by diaphoresis, nausea, dyspnea, and sometimes syncope. Atypical presentations occur in women, elderly, and diabetics. ECG changes and cardiac biomarkers confirm diagnosis. **Treatment** Immediate reperfusion therapy (primary PCI preferred; thrombolysis when PCI unavailable), antiplatelet agents, anticoagulation, analgesia, oxygen if hypoxic, and beta-blockers. Post-MI care includes statins, ACE inhibitors, cardiac rehabilitation, and secondary prevention measures.

**Obesity (Overweight and Related Metabolic Disease) Symptoms** Excess adiposity with increased BMI, often accompanied by metabolic complications—insulin resistance, dyslipidemia, hypertension, obstructive sleep apnea, and increased cardiovascular risk. Psychological and functional impairments are common. **Treatment** Lifestyle interventions (dietary change, increased physical activity, behavioral therapy) are first-line. Pharmacotherapy (GLP-1 receptor agonists, other agents) and bariatric surgery are options for selected patients with severe obesity or comorbidities. Multidisciplinary care addresses nutrition, exercise, psychological support, and long-term follow-up.

**Osteoporosis and Osteopenia Symptoms** Often asymptomatic until fragility fractures occur (vertebral compression, hip, wrist), causing pain, height loss, kyphosis, and disability. Risk factors include age, female sex, low body weight, smoking, glucocorticoid use, and family history. **Treatment** Bone-density testing guides therapy. Calcium and vitamin D supplementation, weight-bearing exercise, fall prevention, and pharmacologic therapy (bisphosphonates, denosumab, selective estrogen receptor modulators, parathyroid hormone analogs) reduce fracture risk. Deformity and reduced mobility occur in advanced disease. **Treatment** Nonpharmacologic measures (exercise, weight loss, physical therapy) are foundational. Analgesics (acetaminophen, NSAIDs), topical agents,

intraarticular corticosteroids, and joint replacement surgery for end-stage disease restore function and relieve pain.

**Pancreatitis (Acute and Chronic) Symptoms** Acute pancreatitis presents with severe epigastric pain radiating to the back, nausea, vomiting, and elevated pancreatic enzymes; severe cases cause systemic inflammatory response and organ failure. Chronic pancreatitis causes persistent pain, malabsorption, steatorrhea, and diabetes. **Treatment** Acute: aggressive IV fluids, pain control, bowel rest, and treatment of underlying causes (gallstones, alcohol). Severe cases require ICU care and management of complications (necrosis, infection). Chronic: alcohol cessation, pancreatic enzyme replacement, pain management, endoscopic or surgical interventions for ductal obstruction, and nutritional support.

**Parkinson Disease Symptoms** Progressive bradykinesia, resting tremor, rigidity, postural instability, and gait disturbance; nonmotor symptoms include autonomic dysfunction, sleep disorders, mood changes, and cognitive decline. **Treatment** Levodopa remains the most effective symptomatic therapy; dopamine agonists, MAO-B inhibitors, and COMT inhibitors are adjuncts. Deep brain stimulation is an option for medication-refractory motor complications. Multidisciplinary care addresses physical therapy, speech therapy, and management of nonmotor symptoms.

**Pneumonia (Community-Acquired and Hospital-Acquired) Symptoms** Fever, productive cough, pleuritic chest pain, dyspnea, and crackles on auscultation; elderly patients may present with confusion or falls. Chest imaging shows lobar or patchy infiltrates. **Treatment** Empiric antibiotics guided by severity, setting (community vs hospital), and risk factors; supportive care includes oxygen, fluids, and respiratory therapy. Vaccination (influenza, pneumococcal) reduces risk. Hospitalization for severe disease and ICU care for respiratory failure or sepsis.

**Prostate Cancer Symptoms** Early prostate cancer is often asymptomatic; later symptoms include urinary hesitancy, weak stream, hematuria, bone pain from metastases, and elevated PSA. Screening and shared decision-making guide detection. **Treatment** Options include active surveillance for low-risk disease, radical prostatectomy, radiation therapy, androgen-deprivation therapy for advanced disease, and systemic therapies (chemotherapy, novel hormonal agents) for metastatic disease. Manage treatment side effects and provide survivorship care.

**Psoriasis Symptoms** Chronic immune-mediated skin disease with well-demarcated erythematous plaques and silvery scale, commonly on extensor surfaces and scalp; may be associated with psoriatic arthritis, nail changes, and systemic inflammation. **Treatment** Topical therapies (corticosteroids, vitamin D analogues), phototherapy, systemic agents (methotrexate, cyclosporine), and biologic therapies (TNF inhibitors,

IL-17/IL-23 inhibitors) for moderate-to-severe disease. Address comorbidities (cardiometabolic risk) and provide patient education.

**Sepsis and Septic Shock Symptoms** Life-threatening organ dysfunction caused by a dysregulated host response to infection—fever or hypothermia, tachycardia, hypotension, altered mental status, oliguria, and laboratory evidence of organ dysfunction. Septic shock includes persistent hypotension requiring vasopressors and elevated lactate. **Treatment** Early recognition and rapid initiation of broad-spectrum IV antibiotics, source control (drainage, debridement), aggressive fluid resuscitation, vasopressors for refractory hypotension, and organ support in ICU. Adherence to sepsis bundles and timely escalation improve outcomes.

**Sexually Transmitted Infections (STIs) Symptoms** STIs produce a range of genital and systemic symptoms—urethral or vaginal discharge, genital ulcers, pelvic pain, dysuria, and systemic signs in disseminated infections. Many infections (chlamydia, gonorrhea, HPV, HIV, syphilis) may be asymptomatic. **Treatment** Diagnosis by testing guides therapy: antibiotics for bacterial STIs (azithromycin/doxycycline for chlamydia, ceftriaxone for gonorrhea, penicillin for syphilis), antivirals for herpes, and counseling, partner notification, and prevention strategies (condoms, vaccination for HPV and hepatitis B). Routine screening in at-risk populations reduces transmission.

**Stroke (Ischemic and Hemorrhagic)** — *See Ischemic Stroke entry above for ischemic management; hemorrhagic stroke requires neurosurgical evaluation, blood-pressure control, reversal of anticoagulation when applicable, and intensive supportive care.*

**Systemic Lupus Erythematosus (SLE) Symptoms** Multisystem autoimmune disease with variable manifestations—malar rash, photosensitivity, arthritis, serositis, renal involvement (nephritis), hematologic abnormalities, and neurologic symptoms. Flares and remissions are typical. **Treatment** Tailored to organ involvement: hydroxychloroquine for most patients, NSAIDs and low-dose corticosteroids for mild disease, and immunosuppressive agents (azathioprine, mycophenolate, cyclophosphamide, biologics) for severe organ-threatening disease. Sun protection, vaccination, and monitoring for complications are important.

**Thyroid Cancer Symptoms** Often presents as a painless thyroid nodule; some patients have hoarseness or compressive symptoms. Most thyroid cancers (papillary, follicular) have favorable prognosis; medullary and anaplastic types are more aggressive.

**Treatment** Surgical thyroidectomy with or without radioactive iodine ablation for differentiated cancers; TSH suppression therapy and long-term surveillance with thyroglobulin monitoring. Multidisciplinary care for advanced or aggressive histologies.

**Tuberculosis (Pulmonary and Extrapulmonary TB) Symptoms** Pulmonary TB: chronic cough, hemoptysis, night sweats, weight loss, and fever. Extrapulmonary TB affects lymph nodes, pleura, bones, CNS, and genitourinary tract with organ-specific signs.

Risk factors include immunosuppression and close contact with infectious cases.

**Treatment** Multi-drug antitubercular therapy (isoniazid, rifampin, pyrazinamide, ethambutol) for active disease with adherence support and monitoring for toxicity. Latent TB infection is treated to prevent progression. Public-health measures include contact tracing and isolation of infectious cases.

**Ulcerative Colitis (Inflammatory Bowel Disease) Symptoms** Continuous mucosal inflammation of the colon causing bloody diarrhea, urgency, abdominal pain, and tenesmus. Severe flares can cause systemic toxicity and risk of toxic megacolon. Extraintestinal manifestations include arthritis and skin lesions. **Treatment** Aminosalicylates for mild disease, corticosteroids for induction of remission, immunomodulators and biologic agents for moderate-to-severe or steroid-dependent disease, and colectomy for refractory disease or dysplasia. Surveillance colonoscopy for cancer risk in long-standing disease.

**Urinary Tract Infection (Cystitis, Pyelonephritis) Symptoms** Cystitis: dysuria, urinary frequency, urgency, suprapubic discomfort, and sometimes hematuria. Pyelonephritis: fever, flank pain, nausea, vomiting, and systemic signs. Elderly patients may present atypically with confusion. **Treatment** Uncomplicated cystitis: short-course oral antibiotics guided by local resistance patterns and symptomatic care. Pyelonephritis and complicated infections require longer courses and sometimes IV antibiotics and hospitalization. Recurrent UTIs prompt evaluation for predisposing factors and preventive strategies.

**Viral Hepatitis** — *See Hepatitis entry above for viral and nonviral causes and treatment approaches.*

**Vertigo and Vestibular Disorders Symptoms** Vertigo is the sensation of spinning or motion, often accompanied by nausea, vomiting, imbalance, and nystagmus. Peripheral causes (benign paroxysmal positional vertigo, vestibular neuritis, Meniere disease) differ from central causes (stroke, multiple sclerosis) by associated neurologic signs. **Treatment** Peripheral vertigo: repositioning maneuvers (Epley) for BPPV, vestibular suppressants short-term, and vestibular rehabilitation. Meniere disease managed with salt restriction, diuretics, intratympanic steroids, or surgical options for refractory cases. Central vertigo requires treatment of the underlying neurologic disorder.

**Viral Infections (General: Dengue, Zika, COVID-19, etc.) Symptoms** Viral infections produce a spectrum from mild febrile illness to severe systemic disease depending on the virus—fever, myalgias, respiratory or gastrointestinal symptoms, rash, and organ-specific complications. Emerging viruses (SARS-CoV-2) can cause severe respiratory failure and multisystem involvement. **Treatment** Supportive care is central for many viral illnesses; specific antivirals exist for some (oseltamivir for influenza,

direct-acting antivirals for hepatitis C, remdesivir for selected COVID-19 cases). Vaccination, vector control, and public-health measures prevent spread. Severe cases require organ support and targeted therapies when available.

**Wound Care and Infection Prevention Symptoms** Wounds range from superficial abrasions to deep lacerations and puncture injuries; signs of infection include increasing pain, erythema, warmth, purulent drainage, and systemic fever. Chronic wounds (venous stasis, diabetic foot ulcers) show delayed healing and risk of osteomyelitis. **Treatment** Initial wound care includes cleansing, debridement of devitalized tissue, appropriate closure when indicated, tetanus prophylaxis, and infection prevention. Infected wounds require targeted antibiotics and sometimes surgical drainage. Chronic wound management uses offloading, vascular assessment, infection control, and advanced dressings or grafting as needed.

Infection during pregnancy can cause congenital Zika syndrome with microcephaly and severe neurologic impairment in the fetus. Guillain-Barré syndrome is a rare neurologic complication. **Treatment** Supportive care—rest, fluids, analgesics, and antipyretics.
